docs.title: 🌐 AgentGrid: Open Agentic Web
docs.text:
AgentGrid is the third generation of agent architectures (Gen-3). It subsumes strengths of Gen-1: AI Agents (autonomous intelligent entities) and Gen-2: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) (distributed problem solvers), while overcoming their limits.

Where Gen-1 solves as lone agent and Gen-2 organizes coordinated teams, AgentGrid operationalizes a decentralized society of agents like the Internet of agents - billions of interconnected agents that can discover each other, negotiate, form ad-hoc collaborations, exchange knowledge, and coordinate actions across open environments.

Key Idea: AgentGrid is foundational infrastructure for the Open Agentic Web - enabling agents to pursue individual and collective goals under shared norms, policies, and guarantees. It transforms isolated agents into participants of a large, cooperative, and dynamic ecosystem that spans trust, adversarial settings, and large-scale distributed problem solving.

docs.title: 🧩 A Simple Analogy
docs.text:
• Gen-1 (AI Agent): Like a skilled individual worker - they can perceive, decide, act, and learn, but they work mostly alone.
  • Gen-2 (MAS): Like a project team - several workers with different roles (planner, doer, verifier) coordinating through set rules to solve a shared problem.
  • Gen-3 (AgentGrid): Like a Civilization - billions of people, organizations, and services interacting freely: forming organizations, coalitions, negotiating contracts, delegating tasks, sharing knowledge, competing and collaborating at scale. No central control, yet society functions through shared norms, infrastructure, and governance.

AgentGrid is this Civilization for AI agents - a digital society where diverse agents can meet, trust, collaborate, and evolve collective intelligence.

🚧 Project Status: Alpha Not production-ready. See Project Status for details.

docs.title: 🌍 AgentGrid as a Digital Civilization
docs.text:
AgentGrid does everything a single agent can do: be goal driven, perceive its environment, reason, plan, decide, act through tools, and learn from feedback to pursue goals under constraints.

It also provides everything a Multi-Agent System (MAS) can do: - Coordinate autonomous agents to achieve outcomes no single agent can. - Solve distributed problems where each agent has incomplete information, no global control, and decentralized data. - Organize agents into roles (planner, doer, verifier, broker), exchanging intents, proposals, and receipts. - Leverage composition, workflows and orchestration. - Collaborate by uniform protocols - Use LLMs as agent “brains,” and tools for actuation.

But AgentGrid goes beyond both. It delivers what an open environment - a true society of agents or Internet of Agents demands:

docs.title: 🌐 What AgentGrid Delivers
docs.text:
AgentGrid integrates with several key projects, each contributing a unique piece of the Open Agentic Web:

Capability Brief Description 🔍 Discovery Agents must find and recognize each other across vast, dynamic networks. 📡 Communication Systems Decentralized communication mesh with diverse channels and messaging for rich, asynchronous, large-scale interaction. 📜 Open Protocols Flexible, interoperable standards for any transaction — no enforced uniformity, since billion-scale ecosystems cannot rely on a single format. 🔐 Trust & Identity Verifiable identity, reputation, and guarantees even in adversarial conditions. 💱 Economy & Exchange Marketplaces, task exchanges, and resource-sharing infrastructures for trade, pricing, and value transfer among agents. 🤝 Negotiation & Contracts Mechanisms to form, validate, and enforce agreements at scale. 🏛️ Collective Governance Norms, institutions, and policy frameworks that balance autonomy with shared order. 🌍 Civilizational Systems Meta-structures (law, culture, governance) that sustain large-scale cooperation across heterogeneous agents. 🔗 Knowledge & Context Sharing Seamless exchange of data, context, and insights across diverse agents and environments. 👥 Agency & Coalitions Ability for agents to join or form agencies, roles, groups, and alliances for common or competitive goals. 🧭 Strategies Decision & Behavior Adaptive mechanisms for deliberation, decision, competition, cooperation, or divergence in complex settings. ⚖️ Scalability Billions of heterogeneous agents interacting without central control.

docs.title: 🏗️ Core Building Blocks of AgentGrid
docs.text:
The AgentGrid is not a single system but a constellation of key projects that together form the foundation of the Open Agentic Web.

The AgentGrid is built upon the following key projects, each contributing a unique piece of the Open Agentic Web:

Project Intuitive Brief 🤖 AIOS Operating system for AI & agents; runtime, orchestration, and execution environment. 🛡️ PolicyGrid Trust and governance layer; aligns AI & agents with shared norms, ethics, and rules. 🎮 OpenArcade Framework to shape agent populations; enables strategies for interaction, collaboration, cooperation, negotiation, and social decision-making. 🔌 ServiceGrid Service, tool discovery and composition; connects agents to distributed services & tools. 🔐 Xchange.id Decentralized task exchange for agents & AI; routes tasks to specialist agents or agencies. 🌐 OpenMe.sh Open, protocol-native communication mesh; enables signaling, message exchange, and shared context across groups, orgs, and geographies. 📜 ContractGr.id Contracts and agreements for AI-first society; formalizes negotiation, commitments, and enforcement. 🔗 Pervasive.Link Meta-protocol that binds heterogeneous systems; encodes, translates protocols, context, languages, and strategies into interoperable structures. 🚉 OpenHub.ai Market hub for decentralized intelligence; backbone for sourcing, distribution, and routing of networked intelligence. 🏛️ AgencyGr.id Societal layer; defines roles, structures, and institutions for collective organization.

docs.text:
• Nested workflow driven planning system
  • Mindlink support - contextually link diverse AI systems as dynamic and on-demand minds for agents.
  • Dynamically creates structured, executable task graphs (PlannerTasks)
  • Supports context-aware, memory-driven planning with MemoryGrid integration

docs.text:

  • Tracks assignment lifecycles and updates via WebSockets and DB watchers
  • Supports automated and human-in-the-loop verification with real-time response handling
  • Integrates constraint validation and deadline expiry logic for robust fault handling

docs.title: ⚙️ Modular Execution Engine
docs.text:
• Executes validated task DAGs & cyclic graphs with support for parallelism and recursion
  • Dynamically dispatches to tool executors, LLMs, DSL workflows, or agent APIs
  • Sandboxed code execution for runtime-generated Python logic
  • Retry, fallback, and dry-run estimation modes supported

docs.title: 🧰 Registry-Driven Tool & DSL Ecosystem
docs.text:
• Unified registry for tools, functions, and DSL workflows
  • Supports remote REST/gRPC-based tools and local logic executors
  • Provides searchable metadata & metrics for LLM-based discoverability and selection
  • Allows versioning, validation, and dynamic schema inspection

docs.title: 🧠 LLM & Optimizer Abstraction
docs.text:
• Backend-agnostic support for OpenAI, AIOS blocks over gRPC/REST, AIOS vDAGs, and custom backends
  • Supports optimizer selection, capability estimation, and structured prompt generation
  • Seamless integration with the behavior planner for intelligent flow construction

docs.title: 🔗 Real-Time State, Messaging, and Streaming
docs.text:
• Policy-driven, rate-limited task ingestion over HTTP and NATS, load-balanced to agent instances via Redis
  • Namespace-aware context stores (in-process or Redis, with TTLs) and NATS-broadcast context caching
  • Real-time streaming of task updates, agent status, and delegation events

docs.title: Agent to Agent message conversion system
Introduction
docs.text:
The MessageHandler framework provides a robust, extensible system for validating, transforming, and managing structured communication between distributed AI subjects (e.g., agents, services, components). It enables seamless interoperability through:

  • Schema-driven input/output validation
  • Template-aware DSL execution for data transformation
  • Subject-aware caching and introspection
  • Metadata-rich message type descriptions

This system is designed to support dynamic, runtime-configurable messaging standards across diverse subjects in large-scale, modular AI systems. Each subject defines its communication patterns and supported message types using templates and DSL workflows, which are stored and accessed via a centralized subject registry.

docs.title: Core Capabilities
docs.text:
• Validation: Validates messages against subject-specific input/output templates, supporting nested schemas and field-level constraints.
  • Transformation: Executes DSL workflows to transform messages between subjects using configurable field mappings and metadata.
  • Discovery: Provides structured inspection of supported message types, associated metadata, and registered DSLs.
  • Caching: Uses an in-memory cache to minimize registry queries and ensure fast local access.

Whether you are building an AI coordination network, a message routing system, or a multi-agent orchestration engine, this framework offers a unified interface to manage structured communication effectively.

docs.title: Schema Description
docs.text: This section documents the structure and purpose of the key schemas used in the message validation and communication system.

docs.title: Communication Schema
docs.text: The SubjectCommunication schema defines how a subject communicates, including the protocols it supports and the types of messages it can send or receive.

docs.title: Data Class
docs.text:
@dataclass
class SubjectCommunication:
    protocols: List[Dict[str, Any]]
    message_types: List[MessageType]

    @staticmethod
    def from_dict(data: Dict[str, Any]) -> "SubjectCommunication":
        return SubjectCommunication(
            protocols=data.get("protocols", []),
            message_types=[MessageType.from_dict(mt) for mt in data.get("message_types", [])]
        )

docs.title: Field Descriptions
docs.text: Field Type Description protocols List[Dict[str, Any]] A list of supported communication protocols. Each dictionary may include keys like type, port, path, etc. message_types List[MessageType] A list of message types that the subject can handle, defined by the MessageType schema.

docs.title: Message Type Schema
docs.text: The MessageType schema describes a specific type of communication message, including templates for input and output validation, DSL transformation logic, and metadata.

docs.title: Data Class
docs.text:
@dataclass
class MessageType:
    type: str
    input_template: Dict[str, Any]
    output_template: Dict[str, Any]
    metadata: MessageTypeMetadata
    standard_fields_mapping_input: Dict[str, str]
    standard_fields_mapping_output: Dict[str, str]
    input_dsl_workflow_id: str
    output_dsl_workflow_id: str

    @staticmethod
    def from_dict(data: Dict[str, Any]) -> "MessageType":
        return MessageType(
            type=data["type"],
            input_template=data.get("input_template", {}),
            output_template=data.get("output_template", {}),
            metadata=MessageTypeMetadata.from_dict(data.get("metadata", {})),
            standard_fields_mapping_input=data.get("standard_fields_mapping_input", {}),
            standard_fields_mapping_output=data.get("standard_fields_mapping_output", {}),
            input_dsl_workflow_id=data.get("input_dsl_workflow_id", ""),
            output_dsl_workflow_id=data.get("output_dsl_workflow_id", "")
        )

docs.title: Field Descriptions
docs.text: Field Type Description type str Unique identifier for the message type. input_template Dict[str, Any] A schema that defines the structure and constraints of incoming data. output_template Dict[str, Any] A schema that defines the structure and constraints of outgoing data. metadata MessageTypeMetadata Additional descriptive information such as description, usage docs, etc. standard_fields_mapping_input Dict[str, str] Mapping from standardized field names to keys in the input template. standard_fields_mapping_output Dict[str, str] Mapping from standardized field names to keys in the output template. input_dsl_workflow_id str DSL workflow ID for transforming input from external to internal structure. output_dsl_workflow_id str DSL workflow ID for transforming output from internal to external structure.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Message templates define the expected structure and validation constraints for the input and output of a MessageType. These templates are used by the MessageHandler to verify correctness and by the DSL executor to assist in transformation.

Templates support field-level validation for types, patterns, enumerations, structure, and value constraints. The format is recursive and can express deeply nested schemas for objects and arrays.

docs.title: Writing a Template
docs.text: Each template is a Dict[str, Any], where each key represents a field name, and the corresponding value is a schema dictionary containing validation rules.

docs.title: Supported Validation Fields
docs.text: Field Type Applicable To Description type string All Data type: string, number, boolean, array, object, any. description string All Optional human-readable description of the field. pattern string string Regular expression the string must match. length number string Maximum allowed length of the string. choices array string, number Allowed set of values. min number number Minimum allowed numeric value. max number number Maximum allowed numeric value. max_length number array Maximum number of array elements. items object array Template for validating each item in an array. properties object object Dictionary defining field schemas inside an object. optional boolean All Whether the field is optional (default is false).

docs.title: Example: Agentic Template
docs.text:
This input template could be used by a messaging agent that receives a structured task request:

input_template = {
    "task_id": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Unique identifier for the task",
        "pattern": "^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{8,32}$"
    },
    "priority": {
        "type": "number",
        "description": "Priority level from 1 (low) to 10 (high)",
        "min": 1,
        "max": 10
    },
    "mode": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Execution mode",
        "choices": ["sync", "async", "stream"]
    },
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "description": "Parameter block for the task execution",
        "properties": {
            "temperature": {
                "type": "number",
                "min": 0.0,
                "max": 1.0
            },
            "max_tokens": {
                "type": "number",
                "max": 2048
            },
            "debug": {
                "type": "boolean"
            }
        }
    },
    "tags": {
        "type": "array",
        "description": "Optional search or routing tags",
        "items": {
            "type": "string"
        },
        "max_length": 10,
        "optional": True
    }
}

This template defines:

  • Required scalar fields with pattern, numeric range, and enumeration
  • A nested parameters object with its own validation rules
  • An optional list of tags with a maximum length

docs.title: SubjectsLocalDB
docs.text: SubjectsLocalDB provides an in-memory cache of all subject metadata and communication configurations retrieved from the subject registry. It reduces repetitive API calls by locally storing subject definitions and communication schemas.

docs.title: Class Initialization
docs.text:
SubjectsLocalDB(db_client: SubjectDBAPIClient)
  • db_client: an instance of SubjectDBAPIClient used to fetch subject definitions from the registry.

docs.title: populate_cache()
docs.text:
Fetches all runtime subjects from the registry and populates the internal cache.

local_db.populate_cache()

docs.title: get_runtime_subject(subject_id: str) -> Optional[Subject]
docs.text:
Retrieves a subject by ID from the local cache.

subject = local_db.get_runtime_subject("agent-123")

docs.title: list_runtime_subjects() -> List[Subject]
docs.text:
Returns a list of all cached subjects.

subjects = local_db.list_runtime_subjects()

docs.title: query_runtime_subjects(query: Dict[str, Any]) -> List[Subject]
docs.text:
Filters subjects based on top-level equality conditions. Supports list containment for array fields.

agents = local_db.query_runtime_subjects({"subject_type": "agent"})

docs.title: get_communication_data(subject_id: str) -> Optional[SubjectCommunication]
docs.text:
Parses and returns the SubjectCommunication object from the subject_config["communication"] field.

comm = local_db.get_communication_data("agent-123")

docs.title: get_communications_searchable_fields(subject_id: str) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]
docs.text:
Returns a list of message types and associated templates and metadata for indexing/search purposes.

fields = local_db.get_communications_searchable_fields("agent-123")

docs.title: get_communications_searchable_representation(subject_id: str) -> Optional[str]
docs.text:
Formats the communication metadata into a human-readable string (useful for LLMs or descriptions).

summary = local_db.get_communications_searchable_representation("agent-123")

docs.title: MessageHandler
docs.text: MessageHandler provides schema-aware validation, transformation, and DSL execution utilities for communication between subjects.

docs.title: Class Initialization
docs.text:
MessageHandler(subject_cache: SubjectsLocalDB)
  • subject_cache: an instance of SubjectsLocalDB with preloaded subject data.

docs.title: validate_input_source(message_type: str, data: Dict[str, Any])
docs.text:
Validates data against the input template of the current subject (determined by SUBJECT_ID).

handler.validate_input_source("chat", {"message": "Hello"})

docs.title: validate_output_source(message_type: str, data: Dict[str, Any])
docs.text:
Validates data against the output template of the current subject.

handler.validate_output_source("chat", {"response": "Hi"})

docs.title: validate_input_for_subject(subject_id: str, message_type: str, data: Dict[str, Any])
docs.text:
Validates data as input for the given subject's message type.

handler.validate_input_for_subject("agent-2", "chat", {"message": "Hello"})

docs.title: validate_output_for_subject(subject_id: str, message_type: str, data: Dict[str, Any])
docs.text:
Validates data as output for the given subject's message type.

handler.validate_output_for_subject("agent-2", "chat", {"response": "Hi"})

docs.title: Transformation Methods
docs.text: Each conversion method uses the DSL executor with appropriate input/output templates and field mappings.

docs.title: convert_input_to_source(message_type: str, data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict
docs.text:
Converts raw input into the current subject's expected input format.

converted = handler.convert_input_to_source("chat", {"user_input": "Hello"})

docs.title: convert_output_to_source(message_type: str, data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict
docs.text:
Converts output data into the current subject's expected output format.

converted = handler.convert_output_to_source("chat", {"reply": "Hi"})

docs.title: convert_input_to_target_subject(subject_id: str, message_type: str, data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict
docs.text:
Transforms input data from the current subject to the target subject’s expected format.

converted = handler.convert_input_to_target_subject("agent-2", "chat", {"user_input": "Hi"})

docs.title: convert_output_to_target_subject(subject_id: str, message_type: str, data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict
docs.text:
Transforms output data from the current subject to the target subject’s output format.

converted = handler.convert_output_to_target_subject("agent-2", "chat", {"reply": "Hello"})

docs.title: is_valid_message_type(subject_id: str, message_type: str) -> bool
docs.text:
Checks whether a message type is defined for a subject.

handler.is_valid_message_type("agent-2", "chat")

docs.title: has_input_dsl(subject_id: str, message_type: str) -> bool
docs.text:
Checks if input DSL is defined for the message type.

handler.has_input_dsl("agent-2", "chat")

docs.title: has_output_dsl(subject_id: str, message_type: str) -> bool
docs.text:
Checks if output DSL is defined for the message type.

docs.title: get_input_dsl(subject_id: str, message_type: str) -> Optional[str]
docs.text:
Returns the input DSL workflow ID for a message type.

docs.title: get_output_dsl(subject_id: str, message_type: str) -> Optional[str]
docs.text:
Returns the output DSL workflow ID for a message type.

docs.title: get_all_message_types(subject_id: str) -> List[str]
docs.text:
Returns all supported message types for the subject.

docs.text:

docs.title: DSL Workflows for Message Translation
docs.text:
In a distributed system of AI agents or services, each subject may have its own data representation standards. To enable seamless communication, the MessageHandler supports message translation via DSL workflows.

DSL (Domain-Specific Language) workflows act as transformation bridges that convert input/output data structures between source and target subjects, while preserving semantics and respecting schema constraints.

docs.title: Why DSL Workflows?
docs.text:
Subjects may differ in how they:

  • Name fields (user_input vs message)
  • Structure objects (flat vs nested)
  • Interpret values (enum strings vs numeric codes)

Rather than hard-coding these mappings, DSL workflows provide a declarative, reusable mechanism to encode transformation logic and apply it dynamically at runtime.

docs.title: DSL Workflow Types
docs.text:
Each message type may define two transformation workflows:

Field Purpose input_dsl_workflow_id Transforms incoming messages into the source subject's input format output_dsl_workflow_id Transforms outgoing messages into the target subject's output format

These are stored per MessageType and executed by the MessageHandler as needed.

docs.title: Workflow Execution Context
docs.text:
When a DSL is executed for message translation, the runtime is provided with structured context to support intelligent transformation:

Field Description data The input data to transform message_type The type identifier of the message communication The full SubjectCommunication object of the current subject field_mapping Mapping from standardized fields to subject-specific fields source_template Schema for the source subject's input/output structure target_template Schema for the target subject's input/output structure metadata Human-readable metadata describing the message (description, example, etc.)

This context is injected as part of the addons argument when executing the workflow via:

executor = new_dsl_workflow_executor(
    workflow_id=workflow_id,
    workflows_base_uri=WORKFLOWS_API_URL,
    is_remote=False,
    addons=context
)
result = executor.execute({"data": input_data})

docs.title: Example Use Case
docs.text:
Let’s say we have two agents:

  • Agent A expects: { "user_input": "Hello" }
  • Agent B expects: { "message": "Hello" }

The DSL workflow for translating A’s output to B’s input might contain rules like:

{
  "workflow": {
    "steps": [
      {
        "transform": {
          "output.message": "input.user_input"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

When the MessageHandler calls convert_input_to_target_subject(...), this DSL is executed to reshape the message appropriately.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
• DSL workflows should not embed hardcoded assumptions about external systems.
  • They should rely on the provided field_mapping, source_template, and target_template.
  • Workflows should be reusable across subjects with similar roles or message semantics.
  • Errors in DSL execution should be caught and logged with fallback if needed.

Here is the documentation for the new section:

docs.title: Selecting Message Type
docs.text: In systems with multiple message types per subject, it becomes essential to support discovery, matching, and intelligent selection of message types for a given communication goal. The MessageHandler and SubjectsLocalDB provide utilities for listing, inspecting, and rendering message types into a searchable representation that can be used by humans, scripts, or language models (LLMs).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• Identify the most appropriate message_type for a given subject
  • Present the available types in a structured, searchable form
  • Enable LLMs or rule engines to make automated decisions about message routing

docs.title: get_all_message_types(subject_id: str) -> List[str]
docs.text:
Returns a flat list of all message types defined for a subject.

types = handler.get_all_message_types("agent-123")
# Output: ['chat', 'search_query', 'summarization_request']

docs.title: get_message_type_metadata(subject_id: str, message_type: str) -> Dict[str, Any]
docs.text:
Returns the metadata dictionary for a given message type.

meta = handler.get_message_type_metadata("agent-123", "chat")
# Output: { "description": "Chat response agent", ... }

docs.title: get_communications_searchable_fields(subject_id: str) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]
docs.text:
Returns a list of message types with input/output templates and metadata fields that can be indexed or used in selection logic.

search_fields = local_db.get_communications_searchable_fields("agent-123")
# Output: list of dicts for each message_type

docs.title: Searchable Representation for LLM Selection
docs.text: To support automated reasoning by LLMs or interactive UI selection, the framework provides a formatted, structured textual representation of the available message types.

docs.title: Method: get_communications_searchable_representation(subject_id: str) -> str
docs.text:
Returns a multi-line string that includes:

  • Message type identifier
  • Input and output template summaries
  • Metadata fields: description, usage docs, examples

docs.title: Example Output
docs.text:
Type: chat
  Input Template: {'message': {'type': 'string'}}
  Output Template: {'response': {'type': 'string'}}
  Metadata:
    description: Handles conversational input and produces agent replies
    usage_doc_link: http://docs.aios/agent/chat
    example: {"message": "What's the weather like today?"}

Type: summarization_request
  Input Template: {'content': {'type': 'string'}}
  Output Template: {'summary': {'type': 'string'}}
  Metadata:
    description: Converts long text into short summaries
    usage_doc_link: http://docs.aios/agent/summarize
    example: {"content": "Article text here..."}

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
representation = local_db.get_communications_searchable_representation("agent-123")
print(representation)

This output can be:

  • Indexed for search
  • Embedded into a chat prompt
  • Displayed in a selection UI
  • Fed into an LLM to ask: “Which message type should I use to summarize a document?”

docs.title: Use in Agentic Systems
docs.text:
• Use the searchable representation to dynamically select the best message_type based on user intent
  • LLMs can be used to map user prompts to message types by inspecting their description, input_template, and example
  • Rule engines can select types based on expected field structure and target format

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Agents Association Registry is a dynamic agent registry that manages and tracks runtime subjects (agents, processors, components, etc.) in an intelligent system. Each subject is a versioned, semantically described runtime unit that can be discovered and invoked by the agent.

This registry supports:

  • Fetching and maintaining runtime metadata from a centralized REST API
  • Registering agents by name and subject ID
  • Querying and listing all available runtime subjects
  • Providing LLM-compatible searchable representations for intelligent planners

Each subject includes details like its version, tags, role, supported DSLs, and runtime traits, making it highly suitable for use in autonomous workflows and agent orchestration.

docs.title: Initialize the Registry
docs.text:
from agent_sdk.known_subjects import KnownSubjects

known_subjects = KnownSubjects(base_url="http://runtime-db-service")

docs.title: Add an Agent
docs.text:
# subject_id = "block.image_processor:1.0-stable"
known_subjects.add_agent("image_agent", subject_id)

docs.title: Remove an Agent
docs.text: known_subjects.remove_agent("image_agent")

docs.title: List Registered Agents
docs.text:
agents = known_subjects.list_agents()
for name, subject in agents.items():
    print(f"{name}: {subject.subject_description}")

docs.title: Query All Runtime Subjects (from backend)
docs.text: all_subjects = known_subjects.list_runtime_subjects()

docs.title: Run a Custom Query
docs.text:
query = {"subject_type": "block", "subject_search_tags": ["text", "nlp"]}
results = known_subjects.query_runtime_subjects(query)

docs.title: Searchable Representation
docs.text:
The method get_searchable_representation() returns a list of structured records that describe each known agent. This is particularly useful for use in LLM-based planners and agent selectors.

searchable = known_subjects.get_searchable_representation()

Each entry includes:

Field Description id Unique subject identifier (type.name:version-tag) name Subject name type Subject type (e.g., block, processor, etc.) description Human-readable description of what the subject does tags Semantic search tags traits Execution/environmental traits (e.g., gpu, batching) role Subject's system role (generator, router, evaluator, etc.) schema DSL input schema (if defined) agent_name Name used in the registry (user-defined alias)

This output can be directly used by an LLM planner to select appropriate agents for downstream tasks.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Initialize the registry
known_subjects = KnownSubjects("http://runtime-db-service")

# Register an agent by its unique subject_id
known_subjects.add_agent("text_summarizer", "block.summarizer:1.0-stable")

# View registered agents
print("Registered Agents:")
for name, agent in known_subjects.list_agents().items():
    print(f"{name} -> {agent.subject_description}")

# Get structured view for LLM integration
llm_input = known_subjects.get_searchable_representation()

for entry in llm_input:
    print(f"Agent {entry['agent_name']} - Role: {entry['role']} - Tags: {entry['tags']}")

docs.title: Agent P2P Module — Client Developer Documentation
Introduction
docs.text:
The Agent P2P Module connects agents over one or more meshes — NATS servers that agents join to discover each other and exchange messages. It is provided by PeersManager in the agents SDK (core.p2p). Every agent instance and agent executor creates one automatically.

It supports:

  • Presence — agents announce themselves when they join a mesh, so each agent knows which peers are reachable on which mesh.
  • Events — broadcast an event to every agent on a mesh, or send one to a specific agent.
  • Task messages — send a task to another agent's executor (see Known issues).

docs.title: Configuring Meshes
docs.text:
Meshes are configured when the agent is deployed (allocation.meshes in POST /api/deploy-agent). The deployer passes them to every instance and executor in the MESH_LIST environment variable:

{ "meshes": [ { "mesh_id": "mesh-a", "url": "nats://10.104.140.46:4222" } ] }

On start-up, PeersManager connects to each mesh's NATS URL. It subscribes to these subjects:

NATS subject Subscribed by Carries mesh instances and executors presence (join / remove) and broadcast events <SUBJECT_ID>__events instances and executors events sent to this agent <SUBJECT_ID>__executor the agent executor only task messages for this agent

After subscribing, it publishes {"event": "join", "subject_id": "<SUBJECT_ID>", "peer": <subject spec>} on mesh.

docs.title: Using P2P in an Agent
docs.text:
The SDK creates the manager and exposes it as context.p2p_manager:

from core.agent_executor import AgentResult, AgentTask, Context
from core.main import main


class MyAgent:
    def __init__(self, subject, context: Context) -> None:
        self.subject = subject
        self.context = context

    # Called for every custom event received from any mesh
    def on_event(self, event_name: str, event_data: dict) -> None:
        print("event", event_name, event_data)

    def on_preprocess(self, task: AgentTask):
        return [task]

    def on_data(self, task: AgentTask) -> AgentResult:
        p2p = self.context.p2p_manager

        # Broadcast to every agent on all meshes (or on mesh_ids=[...])
        p2p.broadcast_event_sync("task_started", {"task_id": task.task_id})

        # Send an event to one agent
        p2p.send_event_sync("need_review", {"task_id": task.task_id}, subject_id="reviewer-agent")

        return AgentResult(task_id=task.task_id, job_output={"ok": True})


main(MyAgent)

If the agent class defines on_event(event_name, event_data), the SDK calls it for every custom_event received. Otherwise events are logged.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
p2p.list_meshes()   # {"mesh-a": {"http_url": "...", "nats_url": "nats://..."}}
p2p.list_agents()   # {"reviewer-agent": {"data": <peer subject spec>, "mesh_ids": ["mesh-a"]}}

Messages to a known agent are published only on the meshes where that agent was seen. Messages to an unknown agent go to all meshes.

docs.title: Event message formats
docs.text:
// broadcast_event (subject "mesh")
{ "event": "custom_event", "event_name": "task_started", "event_data": {...}, "subject_id": "<sender>" }

// send_event (subject "<target>__events")
{ "event": "custom_event", "event_name": "need_review", "event_data": {...}, "from_subject_id": "<sender>" }

docs.title: Mesh management
docs.text:
p2p.add_mesh_sync("mesh-b", http_url="http://mesh-b", nats_url="nats://10.0.0.9:4222")
p2p.remove_mesh_sync("mesh-b")
p2p.unregister_sync()      # announce "remove" on all meshes
p2p.close_sync()           # drain and close all connections

Every method has an async counterpart without the _sync suffix (for example await p2p.broadcast_event(...)). The _sync methods run on the manager's background event loop.

docs.title: Task Messages
docs.text:
# Fire-and-forget: publish a task to <subject_id>__executor
p2p.send_sync(task_id="t-1", subject_id="worker-agent", task_data={"text": "hello"})

# Send and wait for a reply
reply = p2p.send_and_wait_sync(task_id="t-2", subject_id="worker-agent",
                               task_data={"text": "hello"}, timeout=30)

The published message is:

{
  "task_id": "t-1",
  "task": { "text": "hello" },
  "origin": { "internal_task_id": "<uuid>", "sender_subject_id": "<SUBJECT_ID>" }
}

send_and_wait waits for an {"event": "reply", "task_id": "<internal_task_id>", "status": "ok" | "error", "data": ...} message. Use reply_sync(...) / reply_error_sync(...) to answer a task manually.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
Task messaging over P2P does not currently complete end to end:

  • The agent executor only accepts messages with "event_type": "task", but send / send_and_wait don't set it. As a result the executor drops the message (pre_process failed).
  • Replies are published on the NATS subject <to_subject_id>, which agent instances don't subscribe to. So send_and_wait waits until its timeout (forever without one).

To call another agent and wait for its result, use the Delegate API (context.delegator.submit_and_wait(...)) instead. Events and presence work as described above.

docs.title: Other Ways to Reach an Agent
docs.text: Mechanism How Notes Delegate API context.delegator.submit_and_wait(subject_id=..., session_id=..., task_id=..., task_data=...) or POST <delegate>/api/submit-and-wait Synchronous request/response through the target's executor (uses AGENT_DELEGATE_URL) Direct hand-off context.direct.submit(to="<subject_id>", session_id=..., task=task, job_data={...}) Sends a task to another agent's executor with the current task's output_ptr, so the other agent replies straight to the original requester Instance WebSocket ws://<instance>:8765 (port from WS_PORT) Send {"id": "1", "task": {"task_id": "t-1", "job_data": {...}}} or {"id": "1", "tasks": [...]}; the reply is {"id": "1", "ok": true, "data": {"results": [...]}}. If WS_BEARER_TOKEN is set, connections must send Authorization: Bearer <token>

docs.title: Agent Chat Server — Client Developer Documentation
Introduction
docs.text: The Agent Chat Server (services/agents/chat-server) is a FastAPI service that lets clients chat with an agent over a WebSocket. Each message is forwarded to the agent through the Delegate API (/api/submit-and-wait). Sessions and messages are stored in PostgreSQL (TimescaleDB when available).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Environment variable Default Description DELEGATE_SERVER_URL http://35.223.239.192:30725 Delegate API base URL DATABASE_URL postgresql:///chatserver PostgreSQL connection URL HOST / PORT 0.0.0.0 / 8080 Listen address LOG_LEVEL INFO Log level

On start-up the server creates the chat_sessions and chat_messages tables (retrying the DB connection for up to about a minute). If TimescaleDB is available, chat_messages becomes a hypertable.

python3 main.py      # or: docker build -t chat-server . && docker run -p 8080:8080 chat-server

docs.title: WebSocket Protocol (/ws)
docs.text:
1. Initialise — the first message must name the agent:

{ "type": "init", "subject_id": "agent-behavioral-code-creator" }

The server creates a session and replies:

{ "type": "session", "session_id": "sess-1a2b3c4d", "subject_id": "agent-behavioral-code-creator" }

Any other first message gets {"type": "error", ...}, and the connection is closed (code 1008).

2. Send tasks — each subsequent message is forwarded to the agent:

{ "type": "message", "task_id": "task-001", "task_data": { "user_request": "Function to add three numbers in python" } }

task_id is optional (generated if missing). task_data becomes the agent's job_data. The server waits up to 120 s for the Delegate API and replies:

{ "type": "response", "task_id": "task-001", "data": { "success": true, "ack": { ... }, "output": { "job_output": { ... }, "...": "..." } } }

On failure it replies {"type": "error", "task_id": "...", "message": "..."}.

3. Keep-alive — {"type": "ping"} → {"type": "pong"}.

Every request, response and error is saved in chat_messages with direction = request / response / error.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text: Method & Path Description GET /health {"status": "ok"} GET /api/sessions?subject_id=<id> List sessions (newest first; up to 500 when not filtered) GET /api/sessions/{session_id} Get a session (404 if not found) GET /api/sessions/{session_id}/messages All messages of a session, oldest first GET /api/subjects/{subject_id}/sessions Sessions of one agent

docs.title: Example Client
docs.text:
import asyncio, json, websockets

async def run():
    async with websockets.connect("ws://localhost:8080/ws") as ws:
        await ws.send(json.dumps({"type": "init", "subject_id": "agent-behavioral-code-creator"}))
        print(json.loads(await ws.recv()))           # {"type": "session", ...}

        await ws.send(json.dumps({"type": "message",
                                  "task_data": {"user_request": "Function to add three numbers in python"}}))
        print(json.loads(await ws.recv()))           # {"type": "response", ...}

asyncio.run(run())

docs.title: Code Generator SDK — Client Developer Documentation
Introduction
docs.text:
The Code Generator SDK (agents_codegen) lets agents generate code with an LLM and, optionally, execute it at runtime.

It provides:

  • Pluggable backends:
    • AIOS — code models served as AIOS blocks, called over REST (AIOSCodeGeneratorAPI).
    • OpenAI — the OpenAI Chat Completions API (OpenAICodeGenerator).
    • Custom — your own subclass of BaseCodeGenerator.
  • A registry (AgentCodeGenerator) for addressing generators by name.
  • Generate-and-execute: generate Python, install its declared dependencies, load it as a module and call a function or method from it.

Markdown code fences (```python … ```) are stripped from generated code automatically.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The SDK lives in libs/codegen-sdk (package agents_codegen). It has no setup.py, so add libs/codegen-sdk to PYTHONPATH or copy the package into your agent. It depends on openai and requests.

docs.title: Import and Setup
docs.text:
from agents_codegen.generator import AgentCodeGenerator
from agents_codegen.aios import AIOSCodeGeneratorAPI, CodeGenerationError
from agents_codegen.custom import BaseCodeGenerator, OpenAICodeGenerator

codegen = AgentCodeGenerator()

docs.title: Using the AIOS Backend
docs.text:
Register a generator backed by an AIOS code model:

codegen.register_new_code_generator(
    name="aios-default",
    model="magistral-small-2506-llama-cpp-block",       # block ID of the model
    inference_server_id="inference-server-1",           # or a direct URL: "http://35.232.150.117:31504"
    aios_url_map={
        "inference_server_url": "http://<inference-server-registry>",
        "blocks_db_url": "http://<blocks-db>",
    },
    system_message=(
        "You are a helpful assistant that writes clean Python 3 code. "
        "Always include a top-level function `def main(*args, **kwargs): ...` that returns the result. "
        "Declare external packages with REQUIREMENTS = [...] or '# requirements: pkg1, pkg2'."
    ),
    overwrite=True,
)
Argument Default Description name — (required) Registry name model — (required) Block ID of the code model inference_server_id — (required) Inference server ID, looked up in the registry; or an http(s):// URL used directly aios_url_map — (required) inference_server_url (registry) and, optionally, blocks_db_url (used to verify the model exists) system_message "" Default system message (falls back to "You are a helpful assistant that provides code examples.") session_id auto Session ID (codegen-<uuid>) overwrite False Replace an existing generator with the same name (otherwise ValueError)

Each call sends POST <inference-server>/v1/infer:

{
  "model": "magistral-small-2506-llama-cpp-block",
  "session_id": "codegen-...",
  "seq_no": 1735689600123,
  "data": {
    "mode": "chat",
    "gen_params": { "temperature": 0.1, "top_p": 0.95, "max_tokens": 4096 },
    "message": "<prompt>",
    "system_message": "<system message>"
  },
  "graph": {},
  "selection_query": {}
}

The code is read from data.reply in the response.

docs.title: Using the OpenAI Backend
docs.text:
from openai import OpenAI

openai_gen = OpenAICodeGenerator(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",          # default
    client=OpenAI(),              # optional; created from OPENAI_API_KEY if omitted
    default_system_message="You write concise, correct Python.",
)
codegen.register_custom_generator(name="openai", generator=openai_gen)

OpenAICodeGenerator sends max_tokens as max_completion_tokens. It does not forward temperature or top_p.

docs.title: Generating Code
docs.text:
code = codegen.generate_code(
    name="aios-default",
    prompt="Write a function `main(a, b)` that returns the element-wise sum of two integer lists.",
    temperature=0.1,
    top_p=0.95,
    max_tokens=4096,
    system_message=None,        # override the generator's default
)
print(code)

AIOS generators also accept seq_no and extra_headers.

docs.title: Generating and Executing Code
docs.text:
generate_and_execute generates Python, prepares it, and calls an entry point:

result = codegen.generate_and_execute(
    name="aios-default",
    prompt="""
Write Python that accepts two lists of integers and returns their element-wise sum using numpy.
Implement `def main(a, b): ...` that returns the summed list.
""",
    function_name="main",                        # default entry point
    args=[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]],
    kwargs={},
    scope_objects={"EXTRA_CONFIG": {"env": "dev"}},   # injected as module globals
    install_deps=True,
)
print(result)   # [5, 7, 9]

Steps:

  1. Generate the code and strip Markdown fences.
  2. Collect dependencies from any of:
    • REQUIREMENTS = ["pkg", "pkg==1.2"]
    • # requirements: a, b==1.2 or # deps: a b==1.2
    • a fenced ```requirements.txt block
  3. Install them with pip install --upgrade when install_deps=True. A failed install raises RuntimeError.
  4. Load the code as a new module (__generated_<uuid>__, registered in sys.modules), after injecting scope_objects as module globals.

  5. Resolve and call the entry point, in this order:

    1. a top-level function named function_name (default main);
    2. else class_name().method_name if both are given;
    3. else the single class in the module that defines __call__ (it is instantiated, and the instance is called).

    Otherwise a RuntimeError is raised.

Generated code runs in the agent's own process with full privileges, and dependency installation modifies the agent's environment. Only enable this for trusted models and prompts.

docs.title: Managing Generators
docs.text:
codegen.list_generators()             # ['aios-default', 'openai']
codegen.has_generator("openai")       # True
gen = codegen.get_generator("openai") # KeyError if missing
codegen.unregister_generator("openai")
codegen.clear_generators()

docs.title: Writing a Custom Backend
docs.text:
Subclass BaseCodeGenerator and implement generate_code. All its parameters are keyword-only.

from typing import Any, Optional
from agents_codegen.custom import BaseCodeGenerator, CodeGenerationError


class TemplateCodeGenerator(BaseCodeGenerator):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs: Any):
        super().__init__(model="template", **kwargs)

    def generate_code(
        self,
        *,
        prompt: str,
        temperature: float = 0.1,
        top_p: float = 0.95,
        max_tokens: int = 4096,
        system_message: Optional[str] = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> str:
        if "sum" not in prompt:
            raise CodeGenerationError("Unsupported prompt")
        return "def main(a, b):\n    return [x + y for x, y in zip(a, b)]\n"


codegen.register_custom_generator(name="template", generator=TemplateCodeGenerator())
codegen.generate_and_execute(name="template", prompt="sum two lists", args=[[1], [2]])   # [3]

BaseCodeGenerator.__init__ takes keyword-only model, session_id, logger and default_system_message, and provides the _strip_markdown_fences() and _effective_system_message() helpers. Only BaseCodeGenerator instances can be registered with register_custom_generator.

docs.title: Agent Config Store
docs.text:
The Agent Config Store is a Redis-backed configuration manager for agent applications. It is provided by the ConfigManager class in the agent_core_libs package, and is built on the CommonCache Redis wrapper from the same package.

It is useful for agents that need runtime-tunable configuration — thresholds, operational modes, feature toggles — shared across processes and instances.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
ConfigManager provides:

  • Layered reads: environment variables → Redis → defaults → caller-supplied default.
  • Typed getters for str, int, float, bool and JSON.
  • Optional TTLs on values.
  • Bulk operations, snapshots and snapshot loading.
  • Change notifications over Redis Pub/Sub, and a watch() helper to react to them.
  • Validation hooks that run before a value is written.
  • Namespacing, so several modules can keep separate key spaces in one Redis.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
ConfigManager and CommonCache are part of agent_core_libs (libs/core-libs), which depends on redis>=5.0.0.

pip install ./libs/core-libs

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
from agent_core_libs.common_cache import CommonCache
from agent_core_libs.config import ConfigManager

docs.title: Creating a Config Manager
docs.text:
First create a CommonCache (a Redis connection with a key namespace), then wrap it in a ConfigManager:

cache = CommonCache(default_url="redis://localhost:6379/0")

config = ConfigManager(
    cache,
    namespace="config",                 # key namespace for this manager
    env_prefix="AGENT_",                # optional: enable ENV overrides
    defaults={"threshold": 0.75, "mode": "auto"},
    validator=None,                     # optional: callable(key, value), raise to reject
    announce_changes=True,              # publish changes over Pub/Sub
)

CommonCache arguments (keyword-only):

Argument Default Description default_url — (required) Redis URL used when url is not given url None Redis URL (overrides default_url) namespace "common" Key prefix separator ":" Separator used between namespace parts decode_responses, socket_timeout, socket_connect_timeout, health_check_interval, max_connections True, 5.0, 5.0, 15, 128 Redis connection settings value_serializer / value_deserializer JSON for non-strings / JSON-or-string How values are encoded

CommonCache pings Redis on creation and raises if Redis is unreachable.

ConfigManager arguments:

Argument Default Description cache — (required) A CommonCache instance namespace "config" Namespace appended to the cache's namespace (with the defaults above, keys are stored as common:config:<key>) env_prefix None If set, get(key) first checks the environment variable <env_prefix><KEY> (upper-cased, . replaced by _) defaults {} Fallback values when a key is not in Redis validator None validator(key, value) is called before each write; raise to reject the value announce_changes True Publish a message on <namespace>::changes for every set/delete

docs.title: Reading and Writing Values
docs.text:
config.set("threshold", 0.9)
config.set("session_token", "abc", ttl=3600)   # expires after 1 hour

config.get("threshold")            # 0.9
config.get("missing", "fallback")  # "fallback"
config.exists("threshold")         # True
config.delete("threshold")         # True if deleted

get(key, default=None) resolves values in this order:

  1. Environment variable <env_prefix><KEY> (only when env_prefix is set). Values from the environment are always strings.
  2. The value stored in Redis.
  3. defaults[key].
  4. The default argument.

docs.title: Typed getters
docs.text:
config.get_str("mode")                 # "auto"
config.get_int("max_workers", 4)
config.get_float("threshold", 0.5)
config.get_bool("enabled", False)      # accepts true/false, 1/0, yes/no, y/n, on/off
config.get_json("routing_rules", {})   # parses JSON strings; returns dicts/lists as-is

get_bool raises ValueError for values it cannot interpret.

docs.title: Bulk Operations and Snapshots
docs.text:
config.set_many({"mode": "manual", "threshold": 0.6})
config.set_many({"temp_flag": True}, ttl=60)        # TTL applied to every key

config.get_many(["mode", "threshold", "unknown"])   # Redis → ENV → defaults per key

config.set_defaults({"retries": 3})                 # add or override defaults

snapshot = config.snapshot()                        # dict of all keys/values in this namespace (Redis only)
config.load_snapshot(snapshot, clear_before=True)   # optionally wipe the namespace first

list(config)                                        # logical key names in the namespace
len(config)                                         # number of keys
config.keys("thr*")                                 # Redis key names matching a glob (including the namespace prefix)

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
llm_config = config.with_namespace("llm")
llm_config.set("temperature", 0.2)

with_namespace(child) returns a new ConfigManager with its own key space under the parent's namespace. It shares the Redis connection, validator and change-announcement setting, but starts with no defaults. If the parent has an env_prefix, the child's prefix is <env_prefix><CHILD>_.

docs.title: Watching for Changes
docs.text:
When announce_changes=True, every set, set_many, delete and load_snapshot publishes a JSON message on the Redis channel <namespace>::changes:

{ "op": "set", "key": "threshold", "value": 0.9, "ttl": null, "ts": 1735689600 }

Subscribe with watch():

def on_change(event):
    print(f"{event['op']} {event['key']} -> {event['value']}")

config.watch(on_change)                 # runs a daemon thread; returns the Thread

for event in config.watch(None, run_in_thread=False):   # or iterate as a generator
    print(event)

Any instance of the agent that shares the Redis and namespace receives these events. You can use them to reload settings at runtime.

docs.title: Usage Example
docs.text:
from agent_core_libs.common_cache import CommonCache
from agent_core_libs.config import ConfigManager


def validate(key, value):
    if key == "threshold" and not (0.0 <= float(value) <= 1.0):
        raise ValueError("threshold must be between 0 and 1")


cache = CommonCache(default_url="redis://localhost:6379/0", namespace="agent-123")
config = ConfigManager(
    cache,
    env_prefix="AGENT_",
    defaults={"threshold": 0.5, "enabled": True},
    validator=validate,
)


class ThresholdModule:
    def __init__(self, config: ConfigManager):
        self.config = config
        self.threshold = config.get_float("threshold")
        config.watch(self._on_change)

    def _on_change(self, event):
        if event["key"] == "threshold":
            self.threshold = float(event["value"])


module = ThresholdModule(config)
config.set("threshold", 0.8)    # every watcher sees the change

docs.title: Agent Creation — Subject Creation & Deployment
docs.text:
Creating a running agent has three steps:

  1. Create a Subject — store the agent specification in the subjects service.
  2. Register an Agent Deployer — install the deployer into a Kubernetes cluster (once per cluster).
  3. Deploy the Agent — ask the deployer to run the agent's executor and instances. This creates a Runtime Subject that records where the agent is running.

All endpoints below are served by the subjects service. Every response has the shape { "success": <bool>, "data": ..., "message": "..." }.

Set a base variable (optional):

export SUBJECT_DB_URL="http://<subjects-service-host>:<port>"

docs.title: 1) Create a Subject
docs.text: The body is a full Agent Specification. identity.subject_version is required. Set info.container_image_name to the agent's container image — the deployer runs this image for each agent instance.

docs.title: Minimal payload
docs.text:
curl -sS -X POST "$SUBJECT_DB_URL/api/subjects" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "identity": {
      "subject_id": "policy-researcher-1",
      "subject_name": "Policy Researcher",
      "subject_type": "researcher",
      "subject_version": { "version": "1.0.0", "release_tag": "stable" }
    },
    "info": {
      "container_image_name": "registry.example.org/agents/policy-researcher:latest"
    },
    "metadata": {
      "subject_description": "Analyzes policy proposals and drafts briefs",
      "subject_search_tags": ["policy","analysis"]
    },
    "persona": {
      "role": "Policy Analyst",
      "goal": "Summarize and critique policy drafts",
      "persona": "Pragmatic, neutral, cites sources",
      "default_system_message": "Answer with citations and balanced tone."
    },
    "prompting": {},
    "execution": { "logging_level": "INFO" },
    "integrations": {},
    "runtime": { "resources": { "device": "cpu", "cpu_cores": 1.0, "memory_mb": 2048 } },
    "owner": { "org_name": "ExampleOrg", "owners": ["owner@example.org"] }
  }'

identity.subject_id is optional. If you omit it, the service generates one (a MongoDB ObjectId string). Creating a subject with an existing subject_id fails with HTTP 400.

Example response (HTTP 201) — the stored subject, with all defaults filled in:

{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "identity": {
      "subject_id": "policy-researcher-1",
      "subject_name": "Policy Researcher",
      "subject_type": "researcher",
      "subject_version": { "version": "1.0.0", "release_tag": "stable" }
    },
    "info": { "container_image_name": "registry.example.org/agents/policy-researcher:latest", "...": "..." },
    "metadata": { "...": "..." },
    "persona": { "...": "..." },
    "prompting": { "...": "..." },
    "execution": { "...": "..." },
    "integrations": { "...": "..." },
    "runtime": { "...": "..." },
    "owner": { "...": "..." }
  }
}

docs.title: Other Subject endpoints
docs.text:
Method & Path Description GET /api/subjects/<subject_id> Get a subject (404 if not found) PUT /api/subjects/<subject_id> Replace a subject with a full specification PATCH /api/subjects/<subject_id> Update fields: body { "update": { "identity.subject_name": "New Name" } } DELETE /api/subjects/<subject_id> Delete a subject GET /api/subjects?subject_type=<type>&tags=<a,b>&limit=50&skip=0 List subjects, optionally filtered by type and search tags (any match) POST /api/subjects/query Query with a MongoDB filter: body { "query": {...}, "projection": {...}, "sort": [...], "limit": 50, "skip": 0 } GET /api/subjects/health Health check 
curl -sS "$SUBJECT_DB_URL/api/subjects/policy-researcher-1"

docs.title: 2) Register an Agent Deployer
docs.text:
An agent deployer is a service running inside a Kubernetes cluster that creates agent workloads. Register one per cluster:

curl -sS -X POST "$SUBJECT_DB_URL/api/agent-deployers" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "kubeconfig":          { "...": "kubeconfig of the target cluster, as JSON" },
    "deployer_id":         "deployer-111",
    "deployer_name":       "deployer-111",
    "deployer_cluster_id": "gcp-cluster-2",
    "deployer_public_ip":  "35.223.239.192"
  }'
Field Required Description kubeconfig Yes Kubeconfig (as a JSON object) used to install the deployer into the cluster deployer_id Yes Unique ID of the deployer deployer_name Yes Human-readable name deployer_cluster_id Yes ID of the cluster deployer_public_ip Yes Not checked by the API, but needed. Public IP of a cluster node. The deployer is exposed on NodePort 30777, so its URL becomes http://<deployer_public_ip>:30777. Agent and workflow URLs are built from this IP

The deployer is installed in the agent-deployer namespace. If saving the record fails, the installed Kubernetes resources are rolled back.

Method & Path Description GET /api/agent-deployers?cluster_id=<id>&limit=50&skip=0 List deployers POST /api/agent-deployers/query Query deployers (same body as subject queries) PUT / PATCH /api/agent-deployers/<deployer_id> Replace / update a deployer record DELETE /api/agent-deployers/<deployer_id> Uninstall the deployer (body: { "kubeconfig": {...} }) and delete its record

docs.title: 3) Deploy the Agent
docs.text:
curl -sS -X POST "$SUBJECT_DB_URL/api/deploy-agent/deployer-111" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "subject_id": "policy-researcher-1",
    "allocation": {
      "delegate_api_url": "http://35.223.239.192:30725",
      "instances": [
        { "instance_id": "i1", "subject_id": "policy-researcher-1" },
        { "instance_id": "i2", "subject_id": "policy-researcher-1", "node_selector": { "pool": "cpu" } }
      ],
      "meshes": [
        { "mesh_id": "mesh-a", "url": "nats://10.104.140.46:4222" }
      ]
    }
  }'
Field Required Description subject_id Yes Subject to deploy allocation.instances Yes Agent instances to create. Each needs instance_id and subject_id; node_selector is optional allocation.meshes No P2P meshes (NATS) to join, as { "mesh_id", "url" } allocation.delegate_api_url Yes* Delegate API URL given to the agent instances (AGENT_DELEGATE_URL), used by context.delegator. *Not checked by the API, but agent instances built on the agents SDK fail to start without it

The deployer creates the following in the agents namespace:

  • Agent executor — one Deployment with the executor, a scouter and Redis, exposed through two NodePort services: executor port 9000 and scouter port 10000. The executor receives tasks (/submitTask), applies the subject's policies and load-balances tasks across instances.
  • Agent instances — one Deployment per instance, running the image from info.container_image_name with a Redis sidecar. Each instance gets SUBJECT_ID, INSTANCE_ID, SUBJECT_DB_URL, MESH_LIST, AGENT_DELEGATE_URL and JOB_EXCHANGE_API_URL. It exposes ports 8765 (WebSocket) and 9090 (metrics).

On success a Runtime Subject is stored with runtime_subject_id = subject_id:

{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "runtime_subject_id": "policy-researcher-1",
    "subject_id": "policy-researcher-1",
    "runtime_status": "active",
    "runtime_info": {
      "executor": "http://35.223.239.192:31412",
      "scouter":  "http://35.223.239.192:31413",
      "deployment_data": {
        "executor": { "port": 9000,  "node_port": 31412, "...": "..." },
        "scouter":  { "port": 10000, "node_port": 31413, "...": "..." }
      }
    }
  }
}

runtime_info.executor is the URL the Delegate API uses to send tasks to this agent. Deploying a subject that already has a runtime subject fails with HTTP 400 (the record already exists).

docs.title: Remove an Agent
docs.text:
curl -sS -X POST "$SUBJECT_DB_URL/api/remove-agent/deployer-111/policy-researcher-1"

This removes the agent's executor and related Kubernetes resources and deletes the runtime subject.

docs.title: Querying Running Agents (Runtime Subjects API)
docs.text: Deployed agents are recorded as runtime subjects. Use these endpoints to find where an agent is running.

docs.title: GET /api/runtime-subjects/<runtime_subject_id>
docs.text:
curl -sS "$SUBJECT_DB_URL/api/runtime-subjects/policy-researcher-1"

The response has the same shape as the deploy response above.

docs.title: GET /api/runtime-subjects
docs.text:
List runtime subjects. All query parameters are optional:

Parameter Description subject_id Filter by subject ID runtime_status Filter by status (e.g. active) sort <field>:asc or <field>:desc limit, skip Paging (defaults 50, 0) 
curl -sS "$SUBJECT_DB_URL/api/runtime-subjects?runtime_status=active&limit=20"

docs.title: POST /api/runtime-subjects/query
docs.text:
Query runtime subjects with a MongoDB-style filter. The filter goes in query:

1) Runtime subjects of one subject that are active

curl -sS -X POST "$SUBJECT_DB_URL/api/runtime-subjects/query" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "query": { "subject_id": "policy-researcher-1", "runtime_status": "active" }
  }'

2) Runtime subjects whose ID matches a prefix (case-insensitive)

curl -sS -X POST "$SUBJECT_DB_URL/api/runtime-subjects/query" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "query": { "runtime_subject_id": { "$regex": "^policy", "$options": "i" } },
    "limit": 10
  }'

docs.title: Other Runtime Subject endpoints
docs.text: Method & Path Description POST /api/runtime-subjects Create a runtime subject: { "runtime_subject_id", "subject_id", "runtime_info", "runtime_status" } PUT /api/runtime-subjects/<id> Replace a runtime subject PATCH /api/runtime-subjects/<id> Update fields: body { "update": { ... } } DELETE /api/runtime-subjects/<id> Delete the record only (Kubernetes resources are not removed) GET /api/runtime-subjects/health Health check

docs.title: Agent DSL Manager — Client Developer Documentation
Introduction
docs.text:
The DSL Manager module provides a unified interface to register, describe, and execute DSL-based workflows. It also includes utilities to render LLM-readable task descriptions and to plan which DSL/agent/tool to use for a goal.

It provides:

  • Pluggable workflow backends (local loader / remote registry / custom)
  • Consistent execution API (execute, deploy, execute_command, etc.)
  • LLM-friendly descriptions via DSLPlanner
  • Optional human-in-the-loop through NATS helpers

A typical workflow is:

  1. Declare a DSLItem in the subject spec.
  2. Build/resolve a DSL executor from the item.
  3. Register the executor in DSLWorkflowsManager.
  4. Describe DSLs with DSLPlanner, optionally plan with Planner.
  5. Execute the chosen DSL and collect results/feedback.

docs.title: Registering DSLs in Subject Specification
docs.text: DSLs are registered using a DSLItem.

docs.title: Data Class Reference
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, Any

@dataclass
class DSLItem:
    dsl_type: str                 # e.g. "registry", "local", "remote"
    dsl_workflow_id: str          # workflow identifier/URI
    dsl_parameters: Dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)

dsl_type: Application specific type dsl_workflow_id is the logical route/URI (e.g., "registry:add-workflow@1.0", "local:math.add", "remote://dsl-executor/add"). dsl_parameters carries backend-specific settings (e.g., registry URL, module path, auth headers, timeouts).

docs.title: Minimal Required Configuration
docs.text:
{
  "dsl_type": "registry",
  "dsl_workflow_id": "add-workflow@1.0",
  "dsl_parameters": {
    "registry_url": "http://dsl-registry-service"
  }
}

docs.title: Field Descriptions
docs.text: Field Location Type Description dsl_type root str Loader/executor type: "registry", "local", or "remote". dsl_workflow_id root str Workflow name/URI/version. dsl_parameters root dict Backend-specific config: registry_url, module_path, executor_url, headers, timeout_s, etc.

docs.title: Example in a Subject Specification
docs.text:
{
  "subject_id": "agent-dsl-executor",
  "subject_type": "agent",
  "dsls": [
    {
      "dsl_type": "registry",
      "dsl_workflow_id": "add-workflow@1.0",
      "dsl_parameters": {
        "registry_url": "http://dsl-registry-service",
        "extras": { "x": 10 }
      }
    },
    {
      "dsl_type": "local",
      "dsl_workflow_id": "math.add",
      "dsl_parameters": {
        "module_path": "agents.dsl.math.add",
        "output_module": "default_output"
      }
    },
    {
      "dsl_type": "remote",
      "dsl_workflow_id": "transform.text.summarize",
      "dsl_parameters": {
        "executor_url": "http://dsl-executor.svc.cluster.local:8080/execute",
        "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer $RUNTIME_TOKEN" },
        "timeout_s": 20
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Import and Setup
docs.text:
from agent_sdk.utils.dsl_manager import (
    DSLWorkflowsManager,
    DSLPlanner,
    HumanInteractionClient
)

from agent_sdk.utils.planner import Planner  # LLM-based planning

docs.title: Building an Executor from a DSLItem
docs.text:
def build_executor_from_dsl_item(item: dict):
    dsl_type = item["dsl_type"]
    workflow_id = item["dsl_workflow_id"]
    params = item.get("dsl_parameters", {})

    if dsl_type == "registry":
        # Resolve via Registry service
        registry_url = params["registry_url"]
        return DSLWorkflowsManager(registry_url).get_workflow(workflow_id)

    if dsl_type == "local":
        # Dynamically import & construct local executor
        module_path = params["module_path"]  # e.g. "agents.dsl.math.add"
        from importlib import import_module
        mod = import_module(module_path)
        return getattr(mod, "Executor")(**params)

    if dsl_type == "remote":
        # Wrap a remote HTTP/gRPC executor
        from agent_sdk.utils.remote_dsl import RemoteDSLWorkflowExecutor
        return RemoteDSLWorkflowExecutor(
            executor_url=params["executor_url"],
            headers=params.get("headers"),
            timeout_s=params.get("timeout_s", 15)
        )

    raise NotImplementedError(f"Unknown dsl_type: {dsl_type}")

docs.title: DSLWorkflowsManager
docs.text:
manager = DSLWorkflowsManager("http://dsl-registry-service")

# Register
manager.register_new_dsl_workflow("add_workflow", "add-workflow@1.0", extras={"x": 10})

# Execute (returns output of the workflow's configured output module)
result = manager.execute("add_workflow", {"x": 5}, output_module="default_output")

# Other operations
manager.deploy("add_workflow")             # preload modules / warmup
manager.check_execute("add_workflow")      # dry-run validation
manager.execute_command("add_workflow", "reindex", {"force": True})
wf = manager.get_workflow("add_workflow")  # access underlying executor
all_dsls = manager.list()                  # list registered
search_meta = manager.get_searchable_representation()
manager.unregister_dsl_workflow("add_workflow")

Common parameters

  • name: local alias in the manager’s registry.
  • workflow_id: backing workflow reference (same as dsl_workflow_id).
  • output_module: which terminal output node/module to read from if multiple.
  • extras: optional config passed to executor (e.g., constants, defaults).

docs.title: DSLPlanner
docs.text:
Use DSLPlanner to generate LLM- and human-readable summaries of your available DSLs and how to call them.

planner = DSLPlanner(dsl_workflows_manager=manager)
planner.prepare_dsl_descriptions()                 # scans manager & builds schema overview
planner.add_task_description("Add two numbers")    # free-form task
planner.add_input_conversion({"x": 5})             # example input mapping
full = planner.get_full_description()              # feed to an LLM or show to users
print(full)

What it does

  • Renders each registered DSL’s name, purpose, inputs/outputs, and example calls.
  • Helps LLMs choose between DSLs based on a task description.

docs.title: Planner (LLM-integrated DSL Selector)
docs.text:
Planner composes job metadata + DSL descriptions + agents/tools into a single prompt and calls a behavior controller (LLM) to propose a plan (e.g., “Use add_workflow with inputs {x: 5, y: 8}”).

planner = Planner(
    behavior_controller_url="http://behavior.svc/planner",
    known_subjects=[...],
    tools_functions_registry=[...]
)

planner.set_custom_description("project_type", "NLP utilities")

final_input = planner.generate_final_input(
    job_goal={"intent": "summarization"},
    job_objectives={"accuracy": "high"},
    job_steerability_data={"style": "concise"},
    task_description="Summarize customer reviews"
)

plan_response = planner.create_plan("Summarize customer reviews")

Highlights

  • Prompt construction with job goal/objectives + DSL/agent/tool metadata.
  • Behavior controller call via TaskProcessorClient (implementation detail).
  • Hooks via set_custom_job_transformer for custom formatting/filters.

docs.title: Human Interaction (Optional)
docs.text:
Use these if a workflow requires approval, data fixes, or confirmations:

hic = HumanInteractionClient(nats_url="nats://nats:4222", topic="dsl.human")
# Send question → await response via MessageResponseWaiter (internal utility)

docs.title: Writing a Custom DSL Executor
docs.text:
Implement a simple interface (execute, optional deploy/check_execute/execute_command):

class MyCustomDSLExecutor:
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        ...

    def deploy(self):
        # module preload / cache warmup
        ...

    def check_execute(self, input_data: dict) -> bool:
        # validate inputs; return True/raise
        return True

    def execute(self, input_data: dict, output_module: str = None):
        # perform the workflow logic and return output
        return {"result": ...}

    def execute_command(self, command_name: str, data: dict):
        # custom control-plane actions (e.g., reindex)
        return {"ok": True}

Register with the manager:

executor = MyCustomDSLExecutor(...)
manager.register_new_dsl_workflow("custom.flow", "custom.flow@1.0", extras={"mode": "fast"})
manager.deploy("custom.flow")
out = manager.execute("custom.flow", {"x": 1, "y": 2})

docs.title: Quick Subject Spec Example (two DSLs)
docs.text:
{
  "subject_id": "agent-dsl",
  "subject_type": "agent",
  "dsls": [
    {
      "dsl_type": "registry",
      "dsl_workflow_id": "add-workflow@1.0",
      "dsl_parameters": {
        "registry_url": "http://dsl-registry-service"
      }
    },
    {
      "dsl_type": "remote",
      "dsl_workflow_id": "transform.text.summarize",
      "dsl_parameters": {
        "executor_url": "http://dsl-executor.svc.cluster.local:8080/execute",
        "timeout_s": 20
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Minimal End-to-End Example
docs.text:
# 1) Build executors from DSLItems (e.g., loaded from subject spec)
items = [
    {"dsl_type": "registry", "dsl_workflow_id": "add-workflow@1.0",
     "dsl_parameters": {"registry_url": "http://dsl-registry-service"}},
    {"dsl_type": "remote", "dsl_workflow_id": "transform.text.summarize",
     "dsl_parameters": {"executor_url": "http://dsl-exec:8080/execute"}}
]

manager = DSLWorkflowsManager("http://dsl-registry-service")
for it in items:
    exec_obj = build_executor_from_dsl_item(it)
    alias = it["dsl_workflow_id"]
    manager.register_new_dsl_workflow(alias, it["dsl_workflow_id"])
    # Optionally bind the resolved executor to alias if needed
    # manager.override_executor(alias, exec_obj)

# 2) Describe for LLM
planner = DSLPlanner(manager)
planner.prepare_dsl_descriptions()
planner.add_task_description("Add two numbers")
print(planner.get_full_description())

# 3) Execute
out = manager.execute("add-workflow@1.0", {"x": 5, "y": 7}, output_module="default_output")
print(out)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Agents Embeddings SDK (agents_embeddings) provides one interface for generating embeddings from different backends, and a manager for registering several generators by name.

It provides:

  • Pluggable backends:
    • AIOS — embedding models served as AIOS blocks, called over REST (AIOSEmbeddingsAPI).
    • OpenAI — the OpenAI Embeddings API (OpenAIEmbeddingsGenerator).
    • Custom — your own subclass of BaseEmbeddingsGenerator.
  • Single and batched embedding of texts.
  • Object embedding: embed any object exposing a text representation, keyed by its ID.
  • A registry (AgentEmbeddingsManager) for addressing generators by name.

A typical workflow is:

  1. Declare a ModelItem in the Subject Specification (optional) to record which embeddings model the agent uses.
  2. Create a generator — AIOS-backed or OpenAI/custom.
  3. Register it in AgentEmbeddingsManager.
  4. Generate embeddings for texts or objects.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The SDK lives in libs/embeddings-sdk and depends on openai and requests.

pip install ./libs/embeddings-sdk

docs.title: Registering Embeddings in Subject Specification
docs.text: Embedding models can be recorded in the subject's integrations.models list using a ModelItem.

docs.title: Data Class Reference
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, Any

@dataclass
class ModelItem:
    llm_type: str
    llm_block_id: str
    llm_selection_query: Dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)
    llm_parameters: Dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
{
  "llm_type": "embeddings",
  "llm_block_id": "bge-large-embeddings-block",
  "llm_selection_query": {},
  "llm_parameters": {
    "inference_server_id": "inference-server-1",
    "batch_size": 64
  }
}

docs.title: Field Descriptions
docs.text:
Field Type Description llm_type str Model kind, e.g. "embeddings". llm_block_id str ID of the AIOS block (or provider model name) to use. llm_selection_query dict Optional selector for picking a deployment. llm_parameters dict Backend settings, e.g. inference_server_id, batch_size.

The agents SDK does not build generators from ModelItem entries automatically. Read the entry from self.subject.integrations.models and pass its values to register_new_generator (see below).

docs.title: Import and Setup
docs.text:
from agents_embeddings.embeddings import AgentEmbeddingsManager
from agents_embeddings.aios import AIOSEmbeddingsAPI
from agents_embeddings.custom import BaseEmbeddingsGenerator, OpenAIEmbeddingsGenerator

docs.title: AgentEmbeddingsManager
docs.text:
AgentEmbeddingsManager is a registry of named embeddings generators.

mgr = AgentEmbeddingsManager()

docs.title: Register an AIOS-backed generator
docs.text:
mgr.register_new_generator(
    name="bge",
    model="bge-large-embeddings-block",         # block ID of the embedding model
    inference_server_id="inference-server-1",   # or a direct URL: "http://10.0.0.5:8000"
    aios_url_map={
        "inference_server_url": "http://<inference-server-registry>",
        "blocks_db_url": "http://<blocks-db>",
    },
    default_mode="embedding",
)
Argument Default Description name — (required) Registry name of the generator model — (required) Block ID of the embedding model inference_server_id — (required) Inference server ID, looked up in the registry; or an http(s):// URL used directly aios_url_map — (required) inference_server_url (inference server registry) and, optionally, blocks_db_url (blocks DB, used to verify the model exists) session_id auto Session ID sent with each request (embed-<uuid>) overwrite False Replace an existing generator with the same name (otherwise ValueError) default_mode "embedding" mode value sent to the inference server

Each request is sent to POST <inference-server>/v1/infer:

{
  "model": "bge-large-embeddings-block",
  "session_id": "embed-...",
  "seq_no": 1735689600123,
  "data": { "mode": "embedding", "gen_params": {}, "texts": ["text one", "text two"] },
  "graph": {},
  "selection_query": {}
}

A single text is sent as "message" instead of "texts". The response may carry the vectors in any of data.embeddings, data.embedding (single input), data.data[].embedding or data.reply.embeddings.

docs.title: Register a custom (e.g. OpenAI) generator
docs.text:
from openai import OpenAI

openai_gen = OpenAIEmbeddingsGenerator(
    model="text-embedding-3-small",   # default: "text-embedding-3-large"
    client=OpenAI(),                  # optional; created from OPENAI_API_KEY if omitted
)
mgr.register_custom_generator(name="openai", generator=openai_gen, overwrite=True)

register_custom_generator only accepts instances of BaseEmbeddingsGenerator.

docs.title: Manage generators
docs.text:
mgr.list_generators()          # ['bge', 'openai']
mgr.has_generator("bge")       # True
gen = mgr.get_generator("bge") # KeyError if missing
mgr.unregister_generator("bge")
mgr.clear_generators()

docs.title: Texts
docs.text:
vectors = mgr.embed_texts(
    name="openai",
    texts=["AI is transforming industries.", "Vector databases store embeddings."],
    batch_size=0,     # 0 = one request; > 0 = split into requests of this size
)
# -> List[List[float]], in input order

For AIOS generators you can also pass seq_no, extra_headers, mode and any extra keyword arguments. Extra arguments are sent as gen_params.

docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
Any object with an ID attribute and a method returning its text can be embedded:

class Doc:
    def __init__(self, doc_id, title, body):
        self.id, self.title, self.body = doc_id, title, body

    def get_searchable_representation(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.title}\n{self.body}"

doc_vectors = mgr.embed_objects(
    name="openai",
    objects=[Doc("d1", "Intro LLMs", "Basics of LLMs."), Doc("d2", "Advanced RAG", "Retrieval.")],
    id_attr="id",
    rep_method="get_searchable_representation",
)
# -> {"d1": [...], "d2": [...]}

Generators can also be used directly: gen.embed_texts([...]) and gen.embed_objects([...]).

Errors (failed requests, unexpected response shapes, count mismatches) raise EmbeddingsError.

docs.title: Writing a Custom Generator
docs.text:
Subclass BaseEmbeddingsGenerator and implement embed_texts. embed_objects is inherited.

from typing import Any, List, Sequence
from agents_embeddings.custom import BaseEmbeddingsGenerator


class HashEmbeddings(BaseEmbeddingsGenerator):
    def __init__(self, dims: int = 8, **kwargs: Any):
        super().__init__(model="hash", **kwargs)
