Requires Python ≥ 3.10.

cd agent-memories/Learner
uv venv --python 3.11 .venv && source .venv/bin/activate     # or any Python 3.10+ venv
pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn memorygrid_learner.main:app --port 8000

By default it runs with no external services:

  • SQLite stands in for TiDB.
  • An in-memory vector index stands in for pgvector or Milvus.
  • A local git repo in ./data/lessons_repo holds the lesson files.
  • An offline FakeLLMClient stands in for the LLM when ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is unset.

On start-up the service:

  • starts the filesystem watcher on lessons/ and the database poller;
  • schedules mining runs daily at 02:00, weekly on Sunday at 03:00 and monthly on day 1 at 04:00.

docs.title: Configuration (environment variables)
docs.text:
Variable Default Description MG_TIDB_DSN sqlite+aiosqlite:///./memorygrid_frame.db Lessons/Skills/KB object store. For TiDB use mysql+aiomysql://user:pass@host:4000/framedb MG_VECTOR_BACKEND memory memory, pgvector or milvus MG_VECTOR_DSN "" pgvector DSN or Milvus URI MG_VECTOR_DIM 128 Embedding dimension MG_LESSONS_ROOT ./data/lessons_repo Lesson files + git repository MG_WORKFLOW_STRATEGY statistical Pattern-mining strategy: statistical, llm_only, clustering_llm, custom_dsl MG_DEFAULT_TIME_WINDOW daily Default mining window ANTHROPIC_API_KEY unset Enables real LLM calls (otherwise FakeLLMClient) MG_LLM_MODEL claude-sonnet-5 Model name for LLM calls. Set it to a model ID your account can use (e.g. claude-sonnet-5-5) MG_DSL_CONFIG_DIR ./config/dsl Per-tenant lesson DSL schemas MG_TENANT_ID unset Tenant whose DSL schema to load MG_DB_POLL_INTERVAL_SEC 30 Database poll interval for new drafts

Optional vector backends need extra packages: psycopg[binary] + pgvector (and CREATE EXTENSION vector) for pgvector, pymilvus for Milvus.

The default vector embedding is a deterministic hashed bag-of-words, not a semantic model. Vector search therefore matches on shared words. Pass your own embedding_fn to VectorStoreClient for semantic search (see Programmatic Use).

docs.title: Inject a lesson — POST /lessons/inject/
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/lessons/inject/ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "title": "Retry flaky uploads",
  "body_md": "Retry uploads up to 3 times with exponential backoff when the storage API returns 503.",
  "injector_type": "human",
  "injected_by": "alice@example.com",
  "dsl_payload": {"action": "retry_with_backoff", "instruction_template": "Retry {operation} with backoff"},
  "metadata": {"priority": "high", "criticality": 0.8, "suggested_bin": "skills_base", "tags": ["storage"]}
}'
Field Required Description title, body_md Yes Lesson title and Markdown body injector_type Yes human or ai_agent injected_by Yes Human or agent ID dsl_payload No Structured payload. An action (and optional instruction_template) here lets the Incorporator apply the lesson deterministically metadata No priority (low/medium/high/critical), criticality (0–1), suggested_bin (skills_base/knowledge_base), tags, source_pattern_ids. Default: medium priority, 0.5, knowledge_base

Routing:

  • human — trusted. The lesson skips review and is promoted immediately to the bin in metadata.suggested_bin. Response status: promoted.
  • ai_agent — persisted as a draft, enriched, and queued for human review. Response status: pending_review, with enrichment filled in.

POST /lessons/ does the same as POST /lessons/inject/.

docs.title: Human review
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:8000/lessons/review/queue           # lessons with status pending_review

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/lessons/review/<lesson_id>/decide \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"decision": "approve"}'

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/lessons/review/<lesson_id>/decide \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
    "decision": "edit_then_approve",
    "edits": {"title": "Retry uploads with backoff",
              "metadata": {"suggested_bin": "skills_base", "priority": "high"},
              "notes": "Verified against last week'\''s incidents"}
  }'

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/lessons/review/<lesson_id>/decide \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"decision": "reject", "reject_reason": "too specific"}'
Decision Effect approve Promote to the bin in metadata.suggested_bin edit_then_approve Apply edits (title, body_md, metadata.*, notes → dsl_payload.human_notes), then promote reject Set rejected and reject_reason, move the file to archive/. The record is kept, not deleted

Returns the updated lesson (404 if unknown).

docs.title: Lessons CRUD and search
docs.text: Method & Path Description GET /lessons/{lesson_id} Get a lesson GET /lessons/?q=<text>&status=<status>&top_k=10 List lessons (optionally by status). With q, lessons are filtered by text match on title/body, and bin_matches adds the best Skills/KB hits (text + vector) PUT /lessons/{lesson_id} Update title, body_md, metadata (merged); re-writes the file and commits DELETE /lessons/{lesson_id} Delete the lesson record, its vector entry and its Skills/KB entries

docs.title: Cross-agent lesson request — POST /lessons/cross-agent/request
docs.text:
Read-only. A peer agent asks for relevant promoted lessons:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/lessons/cross-agent/request -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"agent_id": "peer-agent-7", "query": "upload retries", "top_k": 5, "bin": "skills_base"}'

The response is {"requested_by": "peer-agent-7", "lessons": [{"lesson_id", "title", "body_md", "score", "match_type": "text" | "vector"}, ...]}. Omit bin to search both bins. Text matches score 1.0.

docs.title: Mining on demand — POST /learner/trigger?time_window=daily
docs.text: Runs the mining pipeline once and returns the new draft lesson. time_window is daily, weekly or monthly.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: Method & Path Returns GET /lessons/metrics/throughput?granularity=day Lessons created per day, week (ISO) or month GET /lessons/metrics/outcomes total, promoted, rejected, pending, graduation_ratio, rejection_ratio GET /health {"status": "ok"}

docs.title: The Mining Pipeline
docs.text:
run_learner_pipeline(time_window):

  1. Data collection — DataCollector gathers episodes, task outcomes and auxiliary records (working memory, reflections) for the window.
  2. Pattern extraction — the configured workflow strategy returns ExtractedPatterns. Each has a pattern_type (recurring_behaviour, failure_mode, successful_strategy or new_correlation), a description, supporting_evidence, a confidence and a time_window. Patterns are saved as extracted_pattern objects.
  3. Lesson creation — LessonDocumentCreator renders a lesson (Markdown + dsl_payload + metadata).
  4. Persist — the lesson file is written to lessons/, its record to the database, and both are committed to git.
  5. The watcher detects the new draft, runs enrichment, and submits it to the review queue.

docs.title: Workflow strategies
Lesson creation
docs.text:
The service uses script mode, a deterministic renderer:

  • Title — the highest-confidence pattern.
  • Body — a summary, steps or facts, and evidence sections.
  • Priority — high if the average confidence is ≥ 0.75, medium if ≥ 0.4, else low.
  • Criticality — the average confidence.
  • Suggested bin — skills_base for successful_strategy/failure_mode, otherwise knowledge_base.

LessonDocumentCreator(mode="llm", llm_client=...) renders lessons with an LLM instead.

docs.title: Enrichment and the lesson DSL schema
docs.text:
Enrichment asks the LLM for why_important, reasons_and_evidence, priority_classification, criticality_classification and bin_suggestion, and stores them in lesson.enrichment. Enrichment and lesson creation are driven by a lesson DSL schema (required fields and sections), loaded per tenant:

  1. <MG_DSL_CONFIG_DIR>/<MG_TENANT_ID>.json, else
  2. <MG_DSL_CONFIG_DIR>/default.json, else
  3. the built-in default (title, summary, priority, suggested_bin, optional tags; sections summary, steps_or_facts, evidence).
{
  "version": "2.0",
  "fields": [
    {"name": "title", "type": "string"},
    {"name": "priority", "type": "enum", "enum_values": ["low", "medium", "high", "critical"]},
    {"name": "owner_team", "type": "string", "required": false}
  ],
  "required_sections": ["summary", "steps_or_facts", "evidence", "rollback"]
}

LessonDSLSchema.validate_payload(payload) returns a list of validation errors (empty if valid).

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Store Contents Object store (TiDBFrameDBClient, table framedb_objects) JSON objects keyed by (obj_type, obj_id): lesson, skill, knowledge_base_entry, extracted_pattern Vector store (VectorStoreClient) Embeddings of promoted lessons, with metadata bin and title Filesystem (MG_LESSONS_ROOT) lessons/ (drafts, pending review), skills/, kb/, archive/; each lesson is <id>.md with JSON front-matter (id, title, status, metadata, enrichment) and the Markdown body Git (GitVersioning, same folder) A commit for every draft, update, promotion and archive. history(path) lists a file's commits; rollback(sha) reverts a commit non-destructively

Promotion (SkillsStore.promote / KnowledgeBaseStore.promote):

  1. Moves the file from lessons/ to skills/ or kb/.
  2. Writes the skill or knowledge_base_entry object.
  3. Upserts the embedding.
  4. Commits to git.

docs.title: Feeding Experience into the Learner
docs.text:
The data collector's sources (EpisodicMemoryClient, TaskLogClient, MemoryDBClient) are in-process, append-only stores. They are not connected to Agentic Memory, and they return all records regardless of the time window. Feed them yourself, or replace them with clients that read your real stores. A replacement only needs an async fetch(time_window) -> list[dict] method.

from memorygrid_learner.api.deps import build_dependencies
from memorygrid_learner.learner.pipeline import run_learner_pipeline

deps = build_dependencies()

# Push experience (e.g. from Agentic Memory episodes)
for ep in mem.episodic.get_by_agent("uploader", limit=200):
    deps.data_collector.episodic_db.add({"action": ep.metadata.get("action"),
                                         "outcome": ep.outcome.value})
deps.data_collector.task_log_db.add({"status": "failure", "error_code": "RATE_LIMIT"})

lesson = await run_learner_pipeline("daily", deps.learner_deps)

A custom source:

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

class AgenticMemoryEpisodes:
    def __init__(self, mem, agent_id):
        self.mem, self.agent_id = mem, agent_id

    async def fetch(self, time_window: str) -> list[dict]:
        days = {"daily": 1, "weekly": 7, "monthly": 30}[time_window]
        since = datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(days=days)
        return [{"action": e.metadata.get("action"), "outcome": e.outcome.value, "content": e.content}
                for e in self.mem.episodic.get_by_agent(self.agent_id, limit=1000)
                if e.created_at >= since]

deps.data_collector.episodic_db = AgenticMemoryEpisodes(mem, "uploader")

docs.title: Programmatic Use
docs.text:
All components can be used without the HTTP layer:

from memorygrid_learner.api.deps import build_dependencies
from memorygrid_learner.config import Settings
from memorygrid_learner.hil.review_service import ReviewDecision
from memorygrid_learner.learner.pipeline import run_learner_pipeline

deps = build_dependencies(Settings(lessons_root="/tmp/lessons", workflow_strategy="statistical"))

draft = await run_learner_pipeline("daily", deps.learner_deps)
enriched = await deps.enrichment_workflow.enrich(draft)
enriched = await deps.lessons_store.update_lesson(enriched, stage="draft")

promoted = await deps.review_service.decide(str(enriched.id), ReviewDecision.APPROVE)
hits = await deps.skills_store.search("rate limit", top_k=3)

To plug in a real embedding model, rebuild the vector client with your own embedding_fn before building the stores, or construct the stores directly:

from memorygrid_learner.storage.vector_client import VectorStoreClient

vector = VectorStoreClient(backend="pgvector", dsn_or_uri="postgresql://...", dim=1536,
                           embedding_fn=my_embed)

docs.title: Notes and Limitations
docs.text:
• Review queue. The queue is in-process. The source of truth for pending reviews is the lesson status (GET /lessons/review/queue), so restarting the service doesn't lose them.
  • Duplicate processing. An ai_agent-injected lesson is briefly stored as a draft before it is enriched. If the database poller runs in that window, the lesson can be enriched and queued twice.
  • Data sources. The time window is not applied by the built-in in-memory data sources.

docs.title: Procedural Memory
docs.text:
Procedural memory answers "how do I do this?" A procedure is a named skill: an ordered list of steps (action, parameters, expected outcome), the situations that should trigger it, and a running record of how often it succeeds.

Use it to store playbooks the agent can look up by situation ("the user wants to send an email") and to prefer the procedures that work best.

docs.title: ProceduralMemory
docs.text: Field Type Default Description name str "" Unique-ish procedure name (lookups use it) content str "" Description (stored as description) trigger_conditions list[str] [] Situations in which to use it steps list[ProcedureStep] [] Ordered steps success_rate float 0.0 Running success rate (0 – 1) use_count int 0 Number of recorded executions updated_at datetime \| None created_at on store

docs.title: ProcedureStep
docs.text:
Field Type Default step_order int 0 action str "" parameters dict {} expected_outcome str ""

Storage: PostgreSQL (procedures + procedure_steps, steps cascade-deleted with their procedure), Weaviate (<prefix>Procedural), ArangoDB (procedural_nodes with step_count, success_rate, use_count).

docs.title: Learn a procedure
docs.text:
with AgentMemory(config) as mem:
    proc = mem.learn_procedure(
        "deploy_service",
        description="Deploy a service to the staging cluster",
        trigger_conditions=["user asks to deploy", "new release tagged"],
        steps=[
            {"action": "run_tests", "parameters": {"suite": "unit"}, "expected_outcome": "tests pass"},
            {"action": "build_image", "parameters": {"tag": "latest"}, "expected_outcome": "image pushed"},
            {"action": "kubectl_apply", "parameters": {"env": "staging"}, "expected_outcome": "pods ready"},
        ],
    )

learn_procedure numbers the steps 0, 1, 2… in list order.

docs.title: Find a procedure
docs.text:
mem.procedural.get_by_name("deploy_service")

for p in mem.procedural.search_by_trigger("ship the new version to staging"):
    print(p.score, p.name, [s.action for s in p.steps])

mem.procedural.get_top_procedures(limit=10)   # by success rate, then use count

search_by_trigger is a vector search over the procedure's name, description and step text. Trigger conditions themselves are not part of the embedded text.

docs.title: Track executions
docs.text:
mem.procedural.record_execution(proc.id, success=True)
mem.procedural.record_execution(proc.id, success=False)

p = mem.procedural.retrieve(proc.id)
print(p.use_count, p.success_rate)   # 2 0.5

record_execution increments use_count and updates the running average: new_rate = (old_rate × old_count + (1 if success else 0)) / (old_count + 1).

docs.title: Update and delete
docs.text:
from agentic_memory.models import ProcedureStep

p.steps.append(ProcedureStep(step_order=3, action="smoke_test", expected_outcome="200 OK"))
mem.procedural.update(p)   # replaces all steps, re-embeds

mem.procedural.delete(p.id)

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Method Description store(memory) -> str Store a procedure and its steps retrieve(memory_id) Load a procedure with its steps search(query, top_k=5) Vector similarity search update(memory) Overwrite fields and replace all steps delete(memory_id) Remove the procedure (steps cascade) record_execution(memory_id, success) Update use_count and success_rate get_by_name(name) First procedure with this name, or None get_top_procedures(limit=10) Best procedures by success rate, then use count search_by_trigger(condition) Vector search for procedures that fit a situation

docs.title: Reflective Memory
docs.text:
Reflective memory answers "what did I learn?" A reflection is an insight the agent draws from its own experience: a lesson, a suggested improvement, how confident it is, and which episode it came from.

Reflections let the agent improve between tasks. Before acting, it can search for relevant lessons, and it can count how often each lesson actually influenced a decision.

docs.title: Model: ReflectiveMemory
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description content str "" The reflection itself lesson str "" The lesson learned improvement_suggestion str "" What to do differently source_episode_id str \| None None Episode that produced the insight confidence float 1.0 applied_count int 0 Times the reflection influenced a decision

Storage: PostgreSQL (reflective_memories), Weaviate (<prefix>Reflective), ArangoDB (reflective_nodes). When source_episode_id is set, an episode_reflection edge is created from the episode node (provenance). The edge is skipped silently if the episode node doesn't exist.

docs.title: Reflect on an episode
docs.text:
from agentic_memory.models import Outcome

with AgentMemory(config) as mem:
    ep = mem.remember_episode("Gave weather for Paris, Texas instead of Paris, France",
                              session_id="s7", agent_id="weather-agent",
                              outcome=Outcome.FAILURE, importance=0.8)

    ref = mem.reflect(
        "I assumed the wrong Paris",
        lesson="Clarify ambiguous location references",
        improvement_suggestion="Ask which city is meant when a name is ambiguous",
        source_episode_id=ep.id,
        confidence=0.9,
    )

docs.title: Use reflections before acting
docs.text:
for r in mem.reflective.search("user asks weather for a city name", top_k=3):
    print(f"{r.score:.3f}  {r.lesson}")
    mem.reflective.mark_applied(r.id)      # this lesson influenced the decision

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
mem.reflective.get_from_episode(ep.id)              # records with source_episode_id == ep.id (PostgreSQL)
mem.reflective.get_reflections_for_episode(ep.id)   # nodes linked from the episode (ArangoDB)
mem.reflective.get_most_applied(limit=10)
mem.reflective.get_above_confidence(0.8)

docs.title: Update and delete
docs.text:
ref.confidence = 0.95
ref.improvement_suggestion = "Ask for the country when the city name is ambiguous"
mem.reflective.update(ref)

mem.reflective.delete(ref.id)

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Method Description store(memory) -> str Store a reflection (+ provenance edge when source_episode_id is set) retrieve(memory_id) Load by ID search(query, top_k=5) Vector similarity search update(memory) Re-embed and overwrite content, lesson, suggestion, confidence, applied count, metadata delete(memory_id) Remove from all backends mark_applied(memory_id) Increment applied_count get_from_episode(episode_id) Reflections whose source_episode_id matches get_most_applied(limit=10) Reflections ordered by applied_count get_above_confidence(threshold=0.8) Reflections with confidence >= threshold get_reflections_for_episode(episode_id) Reflection nodes linked from an episode in the graph

docs.title: Reward Memory
docs.text:
Reward memory answers "what works best?" Each memory is a (state, action, reward) tuple: in this situation the agent did this, and it earned this reward. Tuples are grouped by policy, so separate decision domains don't mix.

Because states are embedded, the agent can ask "in situations like this one, which action earned the most?" even when the new state is worded differently.

docs.title: Model: RewardMemory
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description state_description str "" The situation (also stored as content) action str "" Action taken reward float 0.0 Reward received (any sign or scale) outcome str "" What happened policy str "default" Decision domain context dict {} Extra details

Storage: PostgreSQL (reward_memories, indexed by action and policy), Weaviate (<prefix>Reward), ArangoDB (reward_nodes, with memory_relations edges for state transitions).

docs.title: Record rewards
docs.text:
with AgentMemory(config) as mem:
    ids = []
    for state, action, reward, outcome in [
        ("battery level is critically low", "recharge_now", 1.0, "battery restored"),
        ("battery level is critically low", "continue_task", -1.0, "device shutdown"),
        ("external API rate limit reached", "back_off_60s", 0.9, "requests resumed"),
        ("external API rate limit reached", "retry_immediately", -0.5, "429 error repeated"),
    ]:
        ids.append(mem.record_reward(state, action, reward, outcome=outcome, policy="default").id)

docs.title: Choose the best action
docs.text:
best = mem.reward.get_best_action("device battery is almost empty", policy="default")
if best:
    action, avg_reward = best        # ("recharge_now", 1.0)

How get_best_action(state_description, policy="default", top_k=20) decides:

  1. Vector-search the top_k most similar stored states.
  2. Keep the ones with the given policy. If none match the policy, all candidates are used.
  3. Average the reward per action, and return (action, avg_reward) for the highest average.

It returns None when nothing similar is stored.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
mem.reward.get_action_stats("default")
# {"recharge_now": {"count": 1, "avg_reward": 1.0, "max_reward": 1.0, "min_reward": 1.0}, ...}

mem.reward.get_policy_summary("default")
# {"total": 4, "avg_reward": 0.1, "max_reward": 1.0, "min_reward": -1.0, "unique_actions": 4}

mem.reward.get_top_rewards(limit=3, policy="default")
mem.reward.get_by_policy("default", limit=100)

docs.title: State transitions (graph)
docs.text:
mem.reward.record_transition(ids[0], ids[1], action="recharge_now")
mem.reward.get_successor_states(ids[0])     # reward nodes reached from ids[0]

Transitions are memory_relations edges with relation="state_transition" and the action.

docs.title: Search, update and delete
docs.text:
for rw in mem.reward.search("API throttled too many requests", top_k=3):
    print(rw.score, rw.action, rw.reward)

rw = mem.reward.retrieve(ids[0])
rw.reward = 0.8
mem.reward.update(rw)
mem.reward.delete(rw.id)

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Method Description store(memory) -> str Store a tuple retrieve(memory_id) Load by ID search(query, top_k=5) Vector search over state/action/outcome update(memory) Re-embed and overwrite delete(memory_id) Remove from all backends get_best_action(state_description, policy="default", top_k=20) (action, avg_reward) for the best action in similar states, or None get_action_stats(policy="default") Per-action count / avg / max / min reward get_policy_summary(policy="default") Totals for a policy get_by_policy(policy, limit=100) Tuples of a policy, highest reward first get_top_rewards(limit=10, policy="default") Highest-reward tuples of a policy record_transition(from_id, to_id, action) Add a state-transition edge get_successor_states(memory_id) States reached from a state

docs.title: Semantic Memory
docs.text:
Semantic memory answers "what is true?" Each memory is a fact stored as a subject – predicate – object triple, for example ("Paris", "is_capital_of", "France"), with a confidence and a source.

Besides being searchable, facts build a knowledge graph. Every distinct subject and object becomes an entity node, and every fact becomes an edge between them. The agent can then ask "how is A related to B?" or "what do I know about A?".

docs.title: Model: SemanticMemory
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description subject str "" Entity the fact is about predicate str "" Relationship object str "" Value or related entity confidence float 1.0 How sure the agent is source str "" Where the fact came from content str "" Free text (know_fact defaults it to "subject predicate object") updated_at datetime \| None created_at on store Set to now on every update

Storage: PostgreSQL (semantic_memories), Weaviate (<prefix>Semantic), ArangoDB (semantic_nodes, plus entity_nodes + entity_relations for the knowledge graph).

Entity node keys are the first 16 hex characters of the MD5 of the entity name, so the same name always maps to the same node.

docs.title: Store facts
docs.text:
with AgentMemory(config) as mem:
    mem.know_fact("Paris", "is_capital_of", "France", source="wikipedia")
    mem.know_fact("France", "is_member_of", "European Union")
    mem.know_fact("European Union", "uses_currency", "Euro", confidence=0.95)
    mem.know_fact("Python", "is_a", "programming language",
                  content="Python is a general-purpose programming language")

Each call stores the fact and also creates entity nodes for the subject and object (if new) and an entity_relations edge between them. The edge carries predicate, memory_id and confidence.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
for fact in mem.semantic.search("capital city of France", top_k=3):
    print(f"{fact.score:.3f}  {fact.subject} {fact.predicate} {fact.object}")

docs.title: Exact lookups
docs.text:
mem.semantic.get_by_subject("Paris")                 # all facts about Paris, by confidence
mem.semantic.get_by_predicate("is_capital_of")       # all capital-of facts
mem.semantic.get_triple("Paris", "is_capital_of")    # best (highest-confidence) match or None
mem.semantic.get_above_confidence(0.9)

docs.title: Knowledge graph
docs.text:
mem.semantic.get_neighbors("France")                         # entities France points to
mem.semantic.get_neighbors("France", direction="INBOUND")    # entities pointing to France
mem.semantic.get_neighbors("France", direction="ANY")

path = mem.semantic.find_path("Paris", "Euro")
# shortest outbound path: Paris -> France -> European Union -> Euro

get_neighbors returns entity node dicts ({"_key": ..., "name": ...}). find_path returns the vertices of the shortest outbound path over entity_relations.

docs.title: Update and delete
docs.text:
fact = mem.semantic.get_triple("European Union", "uses_currency")
fact.confidence = 1.0
mem.semantic.update(fact)

mem.semantic.delete(fact.id)

update and delete change the fact record and its semantic_nodes node. Entity nodes and entity_relations edges created at store time are not updated or removed.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Method Description store(memory) -> str Store a fact, create entity nodes and a knowledge-graph edge retrieve(memory_id) Load by ID search(query, top_k=5) Vector similarity search update(memory) Re-embed and overwrite; sets updated_at delete(memory_id) Remove the fact record get_by_subject(subject) Facts with this subject, highest confidence first get_by_predicate(predicate) Facts with this predicate, highest confidence first get_triple(subject, predicate) Highest-confidence fact for the pair, or None get_above_confidence(threshold=0.8) Facts with confidence >= threshold get_neighbors(entity, direction="OUTBOUND") Entities directly connected (OUTBOUND, INBOUND or ANY) find_path(from_entity, to_entity) Shortest outbound path between two entities

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Agent Context Cache is an event-driven, in-memory key-value store for agents. It is provided by the agent_context_cache package in libs/agents-addons. It offers:

  • Fast in-memory storage for low-latency access
  • Lightweight namespace isolation to scope key-value pairs
  • A buffered update system that records every write as an operation and processes it on a background thread
  • NATS-based broadcasting of context updates to a configurable list of topics
  • A small configuration store (topics list, backup flag and backup settings) kept in the cache itself

It is useful for per-agent working state that other agents or services should be notified about.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
Download Image

The diagram shows the full design, including a backup subsystem. The components implemented in agent_context_cache.core are described below. Backup is not implemented yet: the backup flag and settings can be stored and read, but no backup manager is wired in.

docs.title: 1. Context Interface and Primary Storage
docs.text: All reads and writes go through AgentContextCache.get / set (and friends) to an InMemoryContextCache. It is a plain Python dict of namespaces, each holding key-value pairs. Reads are served from it directly. Data lives only in the process's memory and is lost on restart.

docs.title: 2. Configuration and Topic Management
docs.text:
ContextConfigurations stores the cache's runtime configuration as ordinary keys in the config namespace of the same in-memory cache:

Key Meaning topics_list NATS subjects that receive context updates backup_enabled Backup flag (stored only) backup_settings Backup settings dict (stored only)

TopicsListConfig is a thin wrapper that reads and updates the topics list.

docs.title: 3. Buffered Processing and Broadcasting
docs.text:
1. Every set, delete (of an existing key) and clear_namespace (of an existing namespace) records an operation in the ContextBufferQueue, a thread-safe queue. This includes writes to the config namespace.

    json { "operation": "set", "namespace": "default", "key": "user_profile", "value": { "name": "Alice" } }

  2. The ContextUpdateProcessor runs on a daemon thread started by AgentContextCache. It takes operations from the queue one at a time and hands each to the ContextUpdateEventPusher.

  3. The pusher connects to NATS at nats://localhost:4222, publishes the event to every topic in topics_list, and disconnects:

    json { "event_type": "context_update", "sender_subject_id": "<SUBJECT_ID env>", "event_data": { "operation": "set", "namespace": "default", "key": "user_profile", "value": { "name": "Alice" } } }

If no topics are configured, a warning is logged and nothing is published. Errors while publishing are logged, and processing continues with the next operation. Values must be JSON-serializable to be broadcast.

docs.title: Importing the context cache
docs.text:
The components live in agent_context_cache.core:

from agent_context_cache.core.agent_context import AgentContextCache
Component Module Description AgentContextCache agent_context_cache.core.agent_context Main class: wires the cache, configuration, queue, processor and pusher InMemoryContextCache agent_context_cache.core.cache In-memory namespaced store that records operations ContextStoreWrapper agent_context_cache.core.cache GET / SET / DELETE / CREATE_NS wrapper around a cache ContextConfigurations agent_context_cache.core.config Configuration store in the config namespace ContextBufferQueue agent_context_cache.core.context_mgmt Thread-safe queue of operations ContextUpdateProcessor agent_context_cache.core.context_mgmt Background processor that drains the queue TopicsListConfig agent_context_cache.core.topics_pusher Wrapper for managing the topics list ContextUpdateEventPusher agent_context_cache.core.topics_pusher Publishes updates to NATS

Dependencies: nats-py (installed separately; it is not listed in agent_addons' setup.py).

Known issue: topics_pusher.py contains from .config import TopicsListConfig, but config.py does not define TopicsListConfig. Importing topics_pusher — and therefore agent_context, which imports it — currently fails with ImportError until that line is removed.

docs.title: Initialize
docs.text:
from agent_context_cache.core.agent_context import AgentContextCache

ctx = AgentContextCache()

The constructor takes no arguments. It creates the in-memory cache and starts the update processor thread.

docs.title: Store and retrieve context values
docs.text:
# Set a value in the default namespace
ctx.set("user_profile", {"name": "Alice", "age": 30})

# Retrieve it
profile = ctx.get("user_profile")
print(profile)  # {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30}

ctx.get("missing")   # None
ctx.delete("user_profile")

docs.title: Use namespaces for scoped isolation
docs.text:
ctx.set("session_token", "abc123", namespace="auth")
ctx.get("session_token", namespace="auth")  # 'abc123'
ctx.get("session_token")                    # None (default namespace)

docs.title: Manage keys and namespaces
docs.text:
ctx.list_keys()                  # keys in the 'default' namespace
ctx.list_keys(namespace="auth")  # keys in 'auth'

ctx.list_namespaces()            # all namespaces, including 'config'

ctx.clear_namespace("auth")      # removes all keys in 'auth'

Namespaces are created automatically on first access (including get and list_keys).

docs.title: Configure topics and backup
docs.text:
ctx.set_topics_list(["agent.context.updates"])   # must be a list (else ValueError)
print(ctx.get_topics_list())                     # ['agent.context.updates']

ctx.enable_backup()
ctx.set_backup_settings({"interval": 60})        # must be a dict (else ValueError)
print(ctx.is_backup_enabled())                   # True
print(ctx.get_backup_settings())                 # {'interval': 60}
ctx.disable_backup()

To add or remove single topics, use the configuration object directly:

ctx.context_configurations.add_topic("agent.context.audit")
ctx.context_configurations.remove_topic("agent.context.audit")

docs.title: Shutdown
docs.text:
ctx.shutdown()

Known issue: shutdown() calls update_processor.stop_processing(), which does not exist. The method that stops the processor is stop(), and it only stops a thread started with ContextUpdateProcessor.start(). The processor thread is a daemon thread, so it ends when the process exits.

docs.title: How broadcasting works
docs.text:
1. A write (set / delete / clear_namespace) is applied to the in-memory cache.
  2. The operation is queued.
  3. The processor thread publishes a context_update event to every configured topic.

Each publish opens and closes its own NATS connection (nats://localhost:4222). The NATS URL is a ContextUpdateEventPusher constructor argument, but AgentContextCache always uses the default.

docs.title: Listening for updates
docs.text:
import asyncio
import json
import nats


async def main():
    nc = await nats.connect("nats://localhost:4222")

    async def handler(msg):
        event = json.loads(msg.data.decode())
        op = event["event_data"]
        print(f"[{event['sender_subject_id']}] {op['operation']} {op['namespace']}/{op['key']} = {op.get('value')}")

    await nc.subscribe("agent.context.updates", cb=handler)
    await asyncio.Event().wait()

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Using the Building Blocks Directly
docs.text:
The components can also be composed by hand, for example to use a different NATS URL:

from agent_context_cache.core.cache import InMemoryContextCache
from agent_context_cache.core.config import ContextConfigurations
from agent_context_cache.core.context_mgmt import ContextBufferQueue, ContextUpdateProcessor
from agent_context_cache.core.topics_pusher import TopicsListConfig, ContextUpdateEventPusher

queue = ContextBufferQueue()
cache = InMemoryContextCache(buffer_queue=queue)
config = ContextConfigurations(context_cache=cache)
pusher = ContextUpdateEventPusher(TopicsListConfig(config), nats_url="nats://nats.messaging:4222")

processor = ContextUpdateProcessor(buffer_queue=queue, event_pusher=pusher)
processor.start()      # background thread
# ...
processor.stop()

InMemoryContextCache(buffer_queue=None) works as a plain namespaced dict with no broadcasting.

docs.title: AgentContextCache Reference
docs.text:
Method Description set(key, value, namespace="default") Store a value (queued for broadcast) get(key, namespace="default") Get a value, or None delete(key, namespace="default") Delete a key (queued for broadcast if it existed) list_keys(namespace="default") List keys in a namespace clear_namespace(namespace="default") Clear a namespace (queued if it existed) list_namespaces() List namespaces set_topics_list(topics) / get_topics_list() Set / get broadcast topics enable_backup() / disable_backup() / is_backup_enabled() Backup flag (stored only) set_backup_settings(settings) / get_backup_settings() Backup settings (stored only) shutdown() See the known issue above

Attributes: cache, context_configurations, topics_list_config, buffer_queue, event_pusher, update_processor.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This module provides a flexible and extensible framework for managing, querying, and executing LLM (Large Language Model) and optimizer blocks within a distributed AI orchestration environment. The system abstracts over heterogeneous backends (OpenAI, internal gRPC servers, and REST APIs) and provides a unified interface for:

  • Registering known or custom models and optimizers
  • Performing inference using pluggable strategies
  • Interacting with behavioral controllers for task planning
  • Generating human-readable prompts with metadata and schema descriptions
  • Estimating model capabilities before execution

docs.title: Key Goals
docs.text:
• Pluggability: Define backends like OpenAI, AIOS, and OrgLLM using a common interface (LLMInferenceAPI)
  • Extensibility: Add new models and optimizers dynamically, including custom logic
  • Interoperability: Integrate seamlessly with external registries, inference engines, and planning APIs
  • Modularity: Clean separation between block metadata management, inference execution, and planner logic

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Deploying a local or distributed LLM registry and running inference tasks through configurable infrastructure
  • Performing ranking and optimizer selection via LLM-driven prompting
  • Schema-aware task planning, enriched with task metadata and historical descriptions
  • Interfacing with a behavior controller or planner that coordinates multiple agents or components in a workflow

This framework is ideal for AI platforms, orchestration systems, or DSL interpreters that need to incorporate LLMs and optimize execution strategies dynamically.

docs.title: Agent LLM Inference Architecture
docs.text:
The Agent LLM Inference System is a modular AI execution pipeline designed to dynamically discover, plan, and execute LLM (Large Language Model) and optimizer-based tasks across heterogeneous backends. It enables DSL workflows, agents, and behavior controllers to submit requests in natural language or structured formats and routes them through a configurable planning and inference stack. The architecture supports constraint checking, stateful execution, model selection, dynamic prompt construction, and backend-agnostic model execution over REST, WebSocket, and gRPC.

Download Image

docs.title: Input Parsing and Execution Dispatch
docs.text:
At the entry point of the system is the input interface that accepts structured task execution requests, either from external clients or internal agent workflows:

  • Input Interface: Entry for task payloads from DSL agents or user interfaces. Supports default brain selection and agent-specific config bootstrapping.
  • Initial Constraint Checker: Enforces preliminary validation using policy rules or access control logic (e.g., organization-specific ACLs).
  • Initial Input Parser: Normalizes input into structured DSL or inference specifications. Supports execution by DSL action ID or direct model selection.

If a DSL workflow is detected, it’s passed to the workflow executor. If the request is a direct inference, it’s routed to the model selection and planner modules.

docs.title: DSL & Workflow Execution Engine
docs.text:
The system supports dynamic workflows using an embedded DSL executor and associated selectors:

  • DSL Action Verifier: Checks whether the action ID is authorized for the current organization.
  • Intelligence Workflow Executor: Executes the DSL via either a standalone block or a composed DAG.
  • DAG/Workflow Selectors: Parses the DAG or ensemble spec and dispatches it to the appropriate workflow executor.
  • Context Window API Client: Pulls historical context for use in prompt enrichment or memory-aware inference.

These components allow the system to support both standalone models and orchestrated multi-step inference chains.

docs.title: Planner Module & Model Pool Interaction
docs.text:
At the heart of the model selection process is the Planner Module, which includes AI model discovery, ranking, and prompt-based refinement:

  • Agents AI Pool Client API: Retrieves model metadata and availability from the internal agent model pool.
  • Historical Contexts API: Feeds contextual traces into the planner for refined prompt generation or decision branching.

  • Planner Execution Modes:

  • Finetune DSL: Adjusts model configurations or selects block variants based on task characteristics.

  • Search + Retrieve + Finetune: Retrieves matching blocks and dynamically adjusts planning parameters.
  • Plan + Search + Retrieve + Execute: Full planning pipeline for complex queries requiring multiple stages of resolution.

Models can be hardcoded, retrieved using tags, or selected through similarity-based semantic matching.

docs.title: Inference Constraint Pipeline
docs.text:
Before running inference, all requests are validated against execution and policy constraints:

  • Constraint Checker: Evaluates the model's execution feasibility and compliance.
  • Request Parser: Decides the execution flow depending on whether the spec is known, estimated, or incomplete.
  • Inference Specification Receiver: Validated model and block IDs are handed off to the downstream executor.
  • Selected Block Pool: Prepared model pool for execution, possibly influenced by prior estimation or rule checks.

This ensures that resource limits, protocol compliance, and model readiness are enforced before invocation.

docs.title: Inference Execution and Policy Rule System
docs.text:
The actual inference logic is executed using a policy-aware runtime executor:

  • Inference Executor: Executes the request based on the selected model and protocol.
  • AI Inference Policy Rule Executor: Uses a preloaded policy-rule client to determine input handling, retry rules, or fallback strategies.
  • Local State Cache: Maintains batched or streaming inputs, historical output context, and temporal buffers for chained workflows.
  • Policy Rules Cache: Ensures low-latency policy enforcement by caching rules from remote registries.

These modules support deterministic and reproducible inference using rules set at the model, org, or request level.

docs.title: Remote Inference & Webhook Execution
docs.text:
Inference can be routed to external or backend-specific executors via protocol-agnostic interfaces:

  • REST API: Standard POST-based request/response execution.
  • WebSocket Executor: Enables real-time streaming inference and multi-turn conversations.
  • gRPC Executor: High-performance protocol for AIOS/OrgLLM deployments with RunInferenceRequest.

Each backend conforms to the LLMInferenceAPI and can be dynamically plugged in via the KnownLLMs registry.

docs.title: AI Data and Webhook Support Layer
docs.text:
A set of AIOS-native webhooks support runtime operations like similarity search, constraint updates, and resource usage estimation:

  • Similarity Search Module: Used by planners to match models to task descriptions using embedding or tag-based policies.
  • Component Registry Webhook: Loads dynamic blocks and optimizers.
  • Block Metrics Webhook: Updates usage statistics, latency logs, and success rates.
  • Resource Allocation Webhook: Enforces runtime limits or routes inference to compliant infrastructure nodes.

These hooks provide dynamic feedback and model reconfiguration capabilities in real-time.

docs.title: Human Intervention & Agent Configuration APIs
docs.text:
In cases requiring manual oversight or approval:

  • Human Intervention Module: Provides pause-and-continue control during planning or inference if specified by the DSL.
  • Agents DB Webhook: Reads model settings, behavioral policies, or default configurations from the agent’s persistent config database.
  • Agent Default Brain Config: Allows default model, prompt template, and rule loading at startup or fallback.

These features ensure that inference is safe, supervised, and in line with organizational policies when required.

docs.title: End-to-End Flow Summary
docs.text:
1. Input is parsed and validated.
  2. DSL or direct inference is chosen based on input.
  3. If DSL, the workflow executor runs; if direct inference, the planner selects the model.
  4. Constraint and policy rules are enforced.
  5. Inference is executed via REST/WebSocket/gRPC.
  6. Results are optionally cached, logged, or streamed back.
  7. Human intervention or planner interaction is applied as per DSL or org rules.

docs.title: Modules Overview
docs.text:
This section provides a high-level breakdown of the primary modules and classes within the system, outlining their roles and interconnections. The system is modular by design, enabling decoupled interaction between model registries, inference backends, planning utilities, and external APIs.

Module Description Block & Metadata Core data models used to represent LLMs, optimizers, and their associated metadata (tags, descriptions, protocols, etc.). KnownLLMs Manages a registry of known or custom LLM blocks. Provides methods for adding, removing, querying, and running inference. KnownLLMOptimizers Similar to KnownLLMs, but manages optimization blocks that can be dynamically selected for LLM task enhancement. LLMSelectorPlanner Builds textual prompts from available LLM metadata and task descriptions. Used for planner interactions with behavioral controllers. OptimizerSelector Constructs prompts to select optimizers based on task requirements and available optimizer metadata. BlocksQueryManager Provides REST API-based interaction with an external block registry. Supports block fetching, filtering, and similarity search. OrgLLMsManager Handles model registration, unregistration, and lookup in an organizational registry using RESTful endpoints. LLMInferenceAPI (abstract) Defines a standard interface for all LLM inference backends. Ensures consistent access to run_inference, check_execute, and get_current_estimates. OpenAIInferenceAPI Concrete implementation of LLMInferenceAPI using the OpenAI Chat API. AIOSInferenceAPI gRPC-based inference backend used for interacting with AIOS-deployed models via BlockInferenceService. OrgLLMInferenceAPI gRPC-based inference for organizational models, with a focus on RunInferenceRequest. AIOSEstimatorClient Provides HTTP-based estimation and execution validation via /discovery/estimate and /discovery/check_execute. Supports pre-evaluation before actual model execution.

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
The LLM inference subsystem can be imported using 

from agents_sdk.llm import *

Certainly. Here's the cleaned and formal version of the documentation section:

docs.title: Registering and Running Inference on LLM Models
docs.text: The KnownLLMs class provides a central interface for managing and executing registered LLM blocks. These blocks may be retrieved from a remote registry or defined locally with custom inference logic. The class exposes methods to register models, remove them, query metadata, and execute inference in a backend-agnostic manner.

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
from agents_sdk.llm import KnownLLMs

llm_manager = KnownLLMs(
    base_url="http://registry.local",
    adhoc_inference_url="http://inference.local"
)
Parameter Type Description base_url str URL of the external block registry to query LLM metadata and listings adhoc_inference_url str URL of the inference backend for executing registry-based LLMs

docs.title: Registering a Remote Model by ID
docs.text:
Registers a block retrieved from the external registry using its block ID.

llm_manager.add_llm(name="my-llm", block_id="llm-block-123")

docs.title: Registering a Custom LLM
docs.text:
Custom blocks can be manually defined and registered using add_custom_llm.

custom_block_data = {
    "id": "custom-llm-block",
    "blockMetadata": {
        "description": "Custom summarization model",
        "tags": ["summary", "text"]
    },
    "inputProtocols": ["text/plain"],
    "outputProtocols": ["text/plain"]
}

llm_manager.add_custom_llm("my-llm", block_data=custom_block_data)

Alternatively, use create_custom_llm_block to register a block and attach a custom inference implementation:

from agents_sdk.llm_inference import OpenAIInferenceAPI

openai_backend = OpenAIInferenceAPI(api_key="sk-...", model="gpt-4")

llm_manager.create_custom_llm_block(
    id="openai-wrapper",
    description="OpenAI GPT-4 wrapper",
    tags=["openai", "chat"],
    input_protocols=["text/plain"],
    output_protocols=["text/plain"],
    block_inference_object=openai_backend
)

docs.title: Listing and Removing Registered LLMs
docs.text:
# List all registered LLMs
for name, block in llm_manager.list_llms().items():
    print(name, block.to_dict())

# Remove an LLM from the registry
llm_manager.remove_llm("my-llm")

docs.title: Querying Registry Blocks
docs.text:
Fetch and filter blocks based on metadata (e.g., tags or input protocols):

query = {"tags": ["qa"], "inputProtocols": ["text/plain"]}
results = llm_manager.query_blocks(query)

for block in results:
    print(block.id, block.blockMetadata.description)

docs.title: Running Inference
docs.text:
Use run_ai_inference to perform inference on a registered LLM.

response = llm_manager.run_ai_inference(
    name="openai-wrapper",
    input_data={
        "prompts": [
            {"role": "user", "content": "What is quantum computing?"}
        ]
    },
    session_id="session-xyz",
    frame_ptr=b""
)

print(response)

If a custom inference backend (custom_block_inference) is attached, it will be used. Otherwise, the system uses AIOSInferenceAPI to call the ad-hoc inference service.

docs.title: Estimating Execution Feasibility
docs.text:
Use estimate to check model feasibility or pre-execution resource requirements.

result = llm_manager.estimate(
    name="openai-wrapper",
    session_id="session-xyz",
    query={"input_size": 2048}
)

print(result)

This functionality is supported for backends that integrate estimation APIs, such as AIOS.

docs.title: Retrieving Searchable Metadata
docs.text:
To retrieve metadata suitable for search or display:

searchable_data = llm_manager.get_searchable_representation()

for item in searchable_data:
    print(item["id"], item["description"], item["tags"])

This representation includes the model ID, description, tags, input protocols, and output protocols.

Certainly. Below is the official documentation for the Block Query Manager, including usage of filter-based and similarity-based model discovery, followed by integration with the KnownLLMs registry.

docs.title: Discovering Models Using Block Query Manager
docs.text:
The BlocksQueryManager class is responsible for querying model blocks from an external registry or discovery service. It supports two primary discovery mechanisms:

  • Filter-based querying: Finds blocks that meet specific field-level constraints (e.g., tags, input protocols).
  • Similarity-based searching: Uses a ranking policy to return the most relevant models based on dynamic task descriptions and a configured similarity policy.

Discovered models can be programmatically added to the KnownLLMs registry for execution and orchestration.

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
from agents_sdk.llm import BlocksQueryManager

query_manager = BlocksQueryManager(base_url="http://registry.local")
Parameter Type Description base_url str Base URL of the block registry or discovery API

docs.title: 1. Filter-Based Query
docs.text: This query returns models that match specified static attributes such as tags, protocols, or block type.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
conditions = [
    {"variable": "tags", "operator": "IN", "value": ["qa"]},
    {"variable": "inputProtocols", "operator": "==", "value": "text/plain"}
]

blocks = query_manager.filter_data(conditions)

for block in blocks:
    print(block.id, block.blockMetadata.description)

The conditions follow a logical structure and are internally passed to a clusterQuery filter with AND logic.

docs.title: 2. Similarity-Based Search (with Ranking Policy)
docs.text: This query supports similarity search based on a text description of the task, using a ranking policy configured on the server.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
conditions = [
    {"variable": "task_description", "operator": "LIKE", "value": "summarize research paper"}
]

policy_code_path = "policies/similarity_policy.zip"

blocks = query_manager.similarity_search(
    conditions=conditions,
    policy_code_path=policy_code_path
)

for block in blocks:
    print(block.id, block.blockMetadata.description)

docs.title: Filter Payload Structure
docs.text:
{
  "body": {
    "values": {
      "matchType": "cluster",
      "filter": {
        "clusterQuery": {
          "logicalOperator": "AND",
          "conditions": [...]
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Similarity Search Payload Structure
docs.text:
{
  "body": {
    "values": {
      "matchType": "cluster",
      "rankingPolicyRule": {
        "values": {
          "executionMode": "code",
          "policyCodePath": "...",
          "settings": {
            "maxResults": 10,
            "enableCaching": true
          },
          "parameters": {
            "filterRule": { ... },
            "return": 5
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Integrating Discovered Models with KnownLLMs
docs.text: Once blocks are retrieved using filter or similarity queries, they can be registered into the KnownLLMs registry dynamically.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from agents_sdk.llm import KnownLLMs

# Initialize managers
llm_registry = KnownLLMs(
    base_url="http://registry.local",
    adhoc_inference_url="http://inference.local"
)
query_manager = BlocksQueryManager(base_url="http://registry.local")

# Discover models with a filter query
conditions = [{"variable": "tags", "operator": "IN", "value": ["summarization"]}]
discovered_blocks = query_manager.filter_data(conditions)

# Register the discovered blocks
for block in discovered_blocks:
    llm_registry.add_custom_llm(name=block.id, block_data=block.to_dict())

# Run inference using the discovered model
response = llm_registry.run_ai_inference(
    name=discovered_blocks[0].id,
    input_data={"prompts": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the following paragraph..."}]},
    session_id="session-123",
    frame_ptr=b""
)

print(response)

This workflow allows dynamic discovery, registration, and usage of LLM models without predefining them in code.

docs.title: Creating and Registering a Custom LLM Model
docs.text: To support custom backends, the system provides an abstract interface called LLMInferenceAPI. Any custom model implementation must subclass this interface and implement its methods. Once defined, the custom logic can be wrapped in a Block object and registered with KnownLLMs for inference.

docs.title: Step 1: Understanding the LLMInferenceAPI Interface
docs.text:
All backend implementations must inherit from LLMInferenceAPI and implement the following methods:

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from typing import Dict

class LLMInferenceAPI(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    def run_inference(self, input_data: Dict) -> str:
        """
        Execute inference on the model using input data.
        Returns a string result.
        """
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def check_execute(self, query: dict):
        """
        Perform a lightweight execution check (e.g., validation or preview).
        Returns a tuple (success: bool, data: Any).
        """
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def get_current_estimates(self):
        """
        Optionally return resource or usage estimates before full execution.
        Returns a tuple (success: bool, data: Any).
        """
        pass

This interface standardizes how models are accessed, ensuring full compatibility with KnownLLMs.

docs.title: Step 2: Implementing a Custom LLM Backend
docs.text:
Here's an example of a simple custom model that returns a reversed input string.

from agents_sdk.llm_inference import LLMInferenceAPI
from typing import Dict

class ReverseTextLLM(LLMInferenceAPI):
    def run_inference(self, input_data: Dict) -> str:
        text = input_data.get("text", "")
        return text[::-1]  # Reverse the input text

    def check_execute(self, query: dict):
        return True, {"status": "Ready"}

    def get_current_estimates(self):
        return True, {"estimated_latency": "1ms"}

docs.title: Step 3: Creating and Registering the Block
docs.text:
Use the create_custom_llm_block() method from KnownLLMs to wrap your custom implementation in a Block:

from agents_sdk.llm import KnownLLMs
from agents_sdk.llm_inference import ReverseTextLLM

# Initialize KnownLLMs
llm_manager = KnownLLMs(
    base_url="http://registry.local",
    adhoc_inference_url="http://inference.local"
)

# Create the custom block
custom_backend = ReverseTextLLM()

llm_manager.create_custom_llm_block(
    id="reverse-llm",
    description="Reverses the input text",
    tags=["test", "reverse"],
    input_protocols=["text/plain"],
    output_protocols=["text/plain"],
    block_inference_object=custom_backend
)

This registers the model internally as reverse-llm and attaches the custom inference logic.

docs.title: Step 4: Running Inference on the Custom Model
docs.text:
result = llm_manager.run_ai_inference(
    name="reverse-llm",
    input_data={"text": "hello world"},
    session_id="session-001",
    frame_ptr=b""
)

print(result)  # Output: "dlrow olleh"

The KnownLLMs registry automatically routes the inference to the ReverseTextLLM implementation based on its registration.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Agents Planning System is a modular, two-stage task decomposition and execution engine designed to dynamically select and utilize intelligent agents, tools, DSLs, or LLMs to fulfill high-level job goals. The system is powered by a centralized Behavior Controller that uses LLMs to reason about job goals, decompose them into actionable plans, and generate structured inputs for execution.

It consists of:

  1. Stage 1 Planning – Decomposes job-level goals into a list of executable sub-tasks (PlannerTasks).
  2. Stage 2 Planning & Execution – For each sub-task, selects the appropriate execution mechanism (e.g., Agent, Tool, DSL, LLM), prepares the input format, and executes it.

This system is used in decentralized or modular AI infrastructures to offload intelligent decisions to suitable agents or functions in a scalable, pluggable way.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
The Agents Planning System is centered around two key data structures:

  1. PlannerTask – represents an individual executable unit of work.
  2. TaskData – aggregates multiple PlannerTasks and tracks overall planning/execution state.

Both are implemented using Python @dataclasses for structured access and serialization.

docs.title: PlannerTask
docs.text: Represents a single task generated by the planner. It contains metadata for execution, dependencies, schema info, and optional routing fields.

docs.title: DataClass Definition
docs.text:
@dataclass
class PlannerTask:
    task_id: str = field(default_factory=lambda: str(uuid.uuid4()))
    main_task_id: Optional[str] = ""
    description: Optional[str] = ""
    execution_type: Optional[str] = ""
    dependencies: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    tool_id: Optional[str] = None
    function_id: Optional[str] = None
    agent_id: Optional[str] = None
    parameters: Dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    arguments: Dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    instructions: Optional[str] = None
    convertor_code: Optional[str] = None
    estimate_data = None
    mark_replan = False
    status: str = "pending"
    output: Dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    creation_time: datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.utcnow)
    last_update_time: datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.utcnow)

docs.title: Field Breakdown
docs.text: Field Type Description task_id str Unique identifier for the task main_task_id Optional[str] Refers to the parent job or TaskData ID description Optional[str] Human-readable description of the task execution_type Optional[str] Type of execution target: agent, tool, dsl, or llm dependencies List[str] Task IDs that must complete before this task is eligible tool_id Optional[str] ID of the tool (if any) to be executed function_id Optional[str] ID of the function (if relevant) agent_id Optional[str] Target agent ID (if applicable) parameters Dict Task configuration, including sub_type arguments Dict Runtime arguments required by the executor instructions Optional[str] Free-form instruction block (optional) convertor_code Optional[str] Optional code snippet to convert input to schema estimate_data Any Cost/latency estimates (if any) mark_replan bool Flag indicating if replanning is required status str Current status (pending, running, completed, etc.) output Dict Final output from task execution creation_time datetime When the task was created last_update_time datetime Last status update timestamp

docs.title: TaskData
docs.text: Represents an entire planning session, containing multiple PlannerTasks and overall input/output tracking.

docs.title: DataClass Definition
docs.text:
@dataclass
class TaskData:
    task_id: str = field(default_factory=lambda: str(uuid.uuid4()))
    task_input_data: Dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    completed_tasks: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    output_data: Dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    creation_time: datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.utcnow)
    update_time: datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.utcnow)
    planned_tasks: List[PlannerTask] = field(default_factory=list)
    status: str = "pending"
    original_job_data: Optional[Dict] = None

docs.title: Field Breakdown
docs.text: Field Type Description task_id str ID of the entire job or plan task_input_data Dict Initial input provided to the planner planned_tasks List[PlannerTask] List of decomposed tasks (phase 1 output) completed_tasks List[str] IDs of tasks that have completed output_data Dict Aggregated output from the job (if any) creation_time datetime Timestamp when this plan was initiated update_time datetime Timestamp of the last update status str Status of the overall task (pending, in_progress, done, etc.) original_job_data Optional[Dict] The job description before planning began

docs.title: Planning and Execution Flow
docs.text: The Agents Planning System uses a two-stage planning architecture to transform high-level job specifications into executable actions across agents, tools, LLMs, or workflows. Each stage plays a distinct role in abstract reasoning and concrete execution.

docs.title: Stage 1 Planning – Abstract Task Decomposition
docs.text:
Purpose: Stage 1 is responsible for breaking down a job into discrete, logical tasks with metadata indicating how each task should be executed.

Component: Planner

Input:

  • job_goal: The primary objective of the job.
  • job_objectives: Supporting targets or sub-goals.
  • job_steerability_data: Constraints, preferences, or behavioral hints.
  • Resource metadata: agents, tools, LLMs, DSLs.

Process:

  • Uses an LLM via the /process-phase-1-task API of the Behavior Controller.
  • Produces a list of structured PlannerTask instances.

Output:

  • A set of tasks, each with:

  • execution_type: Indicates how the task should be executed (agent, tool, llm, or dsl)

  • parameters: Configuration values for further processing
  • agent_id, tool_id, function_id: Routing metadata
  • description, dependencies, status, etc.

Usefulness in the context of agents:

  • Determines which sub-tasks are suitable for agent execution.
  • Assigns tasks to specific agents based on traits, skills, or declared capabilities.
  • Provides enough metadata to delegate to the correct stage 2 planner.

docs.title: Stage 2 Planning – Task Specialization and Execution
docs.text:
Purpose: Stage 2 is responsible for translating a PlannerTask into a concrete input schema and dispatching it to the appropriate backend executor.

Component: One of the following:

  • AgentsPlanner
  • ToolsPlanner
  • LLMSelectorPlanner
  • DSLPlanner

Input:

  • A PlannerTask from Stage 1
  • Input payload or user-provided runtime arguments

Process:

  • Uses the /process-phase-2-task API of the Behavior Controller.
  • Injects agent/tool-specific metadata, schema information, and transformation logic into the planning prompt.
  • Generates a finalized input format that the backend executor can consume.

Output:

  • A response containing:

  • uid: The selected agent, tool, or function identifier

  • input_data: Input parameters structured according to expected schema

Execution:

  • The selected backend is invoked using:

  • P2P messaging (for agents)

  • Tool execution framework
  • LLM inference client
  • DSL workflow engine

Usefulness in the context of planning:

  • Stage 2 planning refines the task boundaries set by Stage 1.
  • Converts abstract tasks into concrete, executable payloads using available metadata.
  • Ensures the agent or tool receives well-structured, validated, and contextually relevant input.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Stage Role Responsible Component Key Output Stage 1 High-level task decomposition Planner PlannerTask list with execution metadata Stage 2 Task-specific input generation Sub-type planners Structured input for agent/tool/LLM/DSL

Stage 1 answers the question: What tasks need to be done and who should do them? Stage 2 answers the question: How should the task be executed and with what input?

Certainly. Here's the structured documentation for Stage 1 Planning.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Stage 1 Planning is responsible for analyzing a high-level job specification and decomposing it into a set of executable units called PlannerTasks. This process is abstract and declarative—it identifies what needs to be done, the order of execution, and which executor type (e.g., agent, tool, LLM, or DSL) is appropriate for each task.

The planning is LLM-assisted and centralized through the Behavior Controller, which responds to semantic prompts with structured planning output.

docs.title: Component: Planner
docs.text:
The Planner class encapsulates the logic for:

  • Collecting job-specific input (goals, objectives, constraints)
  • Describing available execution resources (agents, tools, LLMs, DSLs)
  • Constructing a planning prompt
  • Submitting the prompt to the Behavior Controller
  • Receiving a structured list of PlannerTask objects

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Name Type Description job_goal dict The overarching goal of the task job_objectives dict Specific measurable outcomes or criteria job_steerability_data dict Guidance data such as constraints, preferences, or limits task_description str Additional contextual description for LLM planning agents list Available agents retrieved from KnownSubjects tools/functions list Available tools and functions from ToolsFunctionsRegistry custom_descriptions dict Optional custom textual notes to inject into prompt

docs.title: prepare_job_data(job_goal, job_objectives, job_steerability_data)
docs.text: Combines and formats the job input into a prompt-ready block.

docs.title: prepare_resources_description()
docs.text: Adds structured descriptions of known agents and tools to the planning prompt.

docs.title: add_task_description(task_description)
docs.text: Adds a textual description of the task to the planning prompt.

docs.title: generate_final_input(...)
docs.text: Calls the above methods in sequence and returns the complete prompt sent to the LLM.

docs.title: create_plan(...)
docs.text: Calls the Behavior Controller’s /process-phase-1-task endpoint with the full prompt. Returns the LLM’s output in parsed dictionary form.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
The output of Stage 1 is a list of serialized PlannerTask objects, each with:

  • A unique task_id
  • A description field

  • Execution metadata:

  • execution_type – e.g., "agent", "tool", "llm", "dsl"

  • parameters – e.g., { "sub_type": "agent", ... }
  • Optional fields like tool_id, agent_id, function_id
  • Dependency metadata
  • Default status = "pending"

These tasks are then forwarded to Stage 2 for execution preparation and dispatching.

docs.title: Behavior Controller Integration
docs.text:
The LLM prompt is sent to the Behavior Controller’s API:

Endpoint: POST /process-phase-1-task Payload:

{
  "search_id": "<uuid>",
  "phase_1_data": {
    "task_input_data": "<structured prompt>",
    "n_history_samples": 0,
    "llm_data": { ... }
  }
}

Response:

{
  "success": true,
  "data": [
    {
      "task_id": "...",
      "execution_type": "agent",
      "parameters": { ... },
      ...
    },
    ...
  ]
}

docs.title: Use Case Example
docs.text:
planner = Planner(
    behavior_controller_url="http://controller.local",
    known_subjects=subject_registry,
    tools_functions_registry=tool_registry
)

planner.set_custom_description("note", "Use only verified agents.")
planner.generate_final_input(
    job_goal={"objective": "Summarize dataset"},
    job_objectives={"quality": "high"},
    job_steerability_data={"time_limit": "2 minutes"},
    task_description="Decompose the summarization job."
)

task_plan = planner.create_plan(
    task_description=planner.get_full_description()
)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Stage 2 Planning takes each individual task from the Stage 1 plan (PlannerTask) and translates it into a concrete, executable input tailored for a specific executor—such as an agent, tool, LLM, or DSL workflow. While Stage 1 answers "what needs to be done and who should do it?", Stage 2 answers "how should it be done and with what input?"

Each task’s execution_type and parameters["sub_type"] determine which Stage 2 planner will handle the task.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• Convert high-level task metadata into detailed, structured input for downstream execution systems.
  • Enrich execution context using schema information, traits, metadata, and task descriptions.
  • Interface with the Behavior Controller's Phase 2 API to guide an LLM in generating well-formed inputs.
  • Return the resolved target identifier (uid) and prepared input (input_data) for direct execution.

docs.title: Key Components
docs.text:
Planner Class Handles Sub-Type Execution Target AgentsPlanner "agent" Agent via P2PManager ToolsPlanner "tools" Tool via execute_tool() LLMSelectorPlanner "llm" LLM via run_ai_inference() DSLPlanner "dsl" DSL via execute()

All planners follow a common structure:

  1. Construct the full planning prompt using resource descriptions, schemas, and task descriptions.
  2. Call /process-phase-2-task via TaskProcessorClient.
  3. Parse the LLM response and return structured execution data.

docs.title: Input to Stage 2 Planner
docs.text:
Each planner consumes:

  • A PlannerTask with execution_type and parameters["sub_type"]
  • Input data (Dict) from the calling execution framework
  • Optional LLM configuration (model name, parameters, etc.)

docs.title: Output from Stage 2 Planner
docs.text:
Each planner returns a dictionary with:

  • uid: Identifier of the agent/tool/llm/workflow to execute
  • input_data: Transformed input ready for direct execution

docs.title: Behavior Controller Integration
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /process-phase-2-task Payload:

{
  "search_id": "<uuid>",
  "phase_2_data": {
    "task_input_data": "<full planning prompt>",
    "n_history_samples": 0,
    "llm_data": { ... }
  }
}

Response:

{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "uid": "<agent/tool id>",
    "input_data": { ... },
    "plan": "<optional reasoning steps>"
  }
}

docs.title: 1. AgentsPlanner
docs.text:
• Describes available agents (ID, traits, schema, description)
  • Provides example input for conversion
  • Delegates final input to P2PManager.send_recv(...)

docs.title: 2. ToolsPlanner
docs.text:
• Describes available tools/functions
  • Provides metadata and input schemas
  • Delegates execution to known_tools.execute_tool(...)

docs.title: 3. LLMSelectorPlanner
docs.text:
• Describes available LLM models
  • Formats input for direct inference
  • Calls known_llms.run_ai_inference(...)

docs.title: 4. DSLPlanner
docs.text:
• Describes available workflows and DSL steps
  • Maps task inputs to schema-defined parameters
  • Calls known_dsls.execute(...)

docs.title: Example Flow
docs.text:
For a task of type agent, the flow would be:

  1. PlanAndExecuteL2 receives a PlannerTask with parameters["sub_type"] = "agent"
  2. Initializes AgentsPlanner
  3. Builds full prompt with agents + schema + description
  4. Sends to /process-phase-2-task

  5. Receives:

  6. uid = "agent-42"

  7. input_data = { "doc": "..." }
  8. Sends to P2PManager.send_recv("agent-42", input_data)

docs.title: Use Case
docs.text:
agents_planner = AgentsPlanner(controller_url)
agents_planner.prepare_agents(agents=known_subjects.get_searchable_representation())
agents_planner.add_task_description("Summarize the following input...")
agents_planner.add_input_conversion({"text": "Full report goes here"})

response = agents_planner.create_plan(
    task_description=agents_planner.get_full_description(),
    llm_data={"model": "gpt-4"}
)

subject_id = response['uid']
input_data = response['input_data']

You're welcome. Here's the structured documentation for sections 6 (Unified Execution Layer), 8 (Execution Backends), and 9 (Usage Examples).

docs.title: Component: PlanAndExecuteL2
docs.text: The PlanAndExecuteL2 class is the execution bridge between planning and action. It takes a single PlannerTask—typically produced by Stage 1—and delegates it to the appropriate Stage 2 planner and executor based on the task’s parameters["sub_type"].

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Select the correct Stage 2 planner (AgentsPlanner, ToolsPlanner, etc.)
  • Construct and send phase-2 prompts to the Behavior Controller
  • Invoke the corresponding execution backend (agent, tool, LLM, or DSL)
  • Return structured output including execution result and, optionally, the generated plan

docs.title: Input
docs.text: Parameter Type Description task PlannerTask The task to execute (must be of type "l2_task") known_llms KnownLLMs Registry of LLMs known_tools ToolsFunctionsRegistry Registered tools and functions known_subjects KnownSubjects Registered agents known_dsls DSLWorkflowsManager Available DSL workflows llm_config dict Optional LLM model config

docs.title: Supported Sub-Types and Routing Logic
docs.text: sub_type Stage 2 Planner Executor Function "agent" AgentsPlanner P2PManager.send_recv(subject_id, input) "llm" LLMSelectorPlanner known_llms.run_ai_inference(...) "tools" ToolsPlanner known_tools.execute_tool(uid, input) "dsl" DSLPlanner known_dsls.execute(uid, input, ...)

docs.title: Method: execute_module(input_data: dict) -> dict
docs.text:
Executes the task using the proper planner and backend, returning a dictionary with:

  • output: result from the target system
  • plan: optional reasoning metadata from the planner (if available)

docs.title: Execution Backends
docs.text: After Stage 2 planning completes, execution is performed by one of the following mechanisms, depending on the task’s sub-type.

docs.title: 1. Agent Execution (P2P)
docs.text:
Trigger: P2PManager.send_recv(subject_id, input_data)

  • Sends the input data to the target agent using a peer-to-peer communication channel.
  • Waits synchronously for a response.
  • Expects agent to process the task and return a {"success": true, "data": ...} payload.

docs.title: 2. Tool Execution
docs.text:
Trigger: known_tools.execute_tool(tool_id, input_data)

  • Executes the specified tool (local function, API wrapper, etc.)
  • Supports input transformation based on schema prepared in planning phase.

docs.title: 3. LLM Execution
docs.text:
Trigger: known_llms.run_ai_inference(name, input_data, session_id, frame_ptr)

  • Selects the LLM to invoke based on planner response.
  • Executes prompt or structured input against the registered model backend.

docs.title: 4. DSL Workflow Execution
docs.text:
Trigger: known_dsls.execute(uid, input_data, output_module="")

  • Invokes a DSL-defined multi-step pipeline.
  • Useful for internal control flow, multi-stage validation, or compound logic execution.

docs.title: End-to-End Usage Example
docs.text:
# Step 1: Define your job inputs
job_goal = {"objective": "Summarize research papers"}
job_objectives = {"accuracy": "high", "summary_length": "short"}
steerability = {"tone": "formal", "max_tokens": 200}

# Step 2: Instantiate the planner and generate a task plan
planner = Planner(
    behavior_controller_url=os.getenv("BEHAVIOR_CONTROLLER_URL"),
    known_subjects=known_subjects,
    tools_functions_registry=known_tools
)
full_description = planner.generate_final_input(
    job_goal=job_goal,
    job_objectives=job_objectives,
    job_steerability_data=steerability,
    task_description="Break this job into tasks for agents or tools"
)
response = planner.create_plan(full_description)

# Step 3: Parse PlannerTask(s) from response
task_plan = [PlannerTask.from_dict(t) for t in response['data']]

# Step 4: Execute each task using PlanAndExecuteL2
for task in task_plan:
    if task.execution_type == "l2_task":
        executor = PlanAndExecuteL2(
            task=task,
            known_llms=known_llms,
            known_tools=known_tools,
            known_subjects=known_subjects,
            known_dsls=known_dsls,
            llm_config={"model": "gpt-4"}
        )
        result = executor.execute_module(input_data={"text": "Paper text..."})
        print(f"Task Output:\n{result['output']}")

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
As workflows become more complex, a flat list of planned tasks is often inefficient to execute. The DAG Optimization module enables intelligent grouping of tasks into SubGraphs—units that can be executed independently or in parallel based on dependency satisfaction.

This is especially valuable in agent-based distributed systems, where tasks can be dispatched to multiple agents simultaneously.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use the optimization module:

  • After Stage 1 planning is complete (you have a TaskData instance)
  • Before Stage 2 planning or execution begins
  • When you want to run tasks in batches or parallel, preserving their dependency order

docs.title: Option 1: LLM-Based Optimizer (OptimizationPlanner)
docs.text:
Use this when:

  • Task dependency structures are non-trivial
  • You want smart grouping decisions (semantic understanding of task purposes)
  • You are fine with slightly longer planning time in exchange for better graph structure

Example:

from agent_sdk.optimization import OptimizationPlanner

optimizer = OptimizationPlanner(llm_api)
subgraphs = optimizer.generate_subgraphs(task_data)

Result: A list of SubGraph objects, each containing tasks and dependencies between subgraphs.

docs.title: Option 2: Manual Rule-Based Optimizer (ManualOptimizer)
docs.text:
Use this when:

  • You want deterministic, fast grouping
  • Task dependencies are simple and straightforward
  • You're debugging or working in resource-constrained environments

Example:

from agent_sdk.optimization import ManualOptimizer

optimizer = ManualOptimizer()
subgraphs = optimizer.generate_subgraphs(task_data.planned_tasks)

docs.title: What Is a SubGraph?
docs.text:
A SubGraph is a lightweight wrapper around a set of PlannerTasks that can be executed as a unit. It includes:

  • A unique subgraph_id
  • List of tasks
  • List of other subgraph IDs it depends on
